subject: Kubernetes
summary: Kubernetes is a declarative control system: a replicated datastore of desired state (etcd behind the API server) plus a population of level-triggered controllers that continuously drive observed state towards it. Everything else -- Deployments, Services, autoscaling, storage binding -- is an instance of that one pattern, which is why interviewers probe it: the platform is easy to use badly, and its failure modes (CrashLoopBackOff, Pending pods, CPU throttling, the endpoint race during a deploy, stuck finalizers) only become predictable once you understand the mechanism underneath. Expect to trace a request end to end, to explain requests vs limits and QoS classes, to debug a pod from its status alone, and to justify probe, rollout, placement and storage choices in production terms. The dividing line between candidates is almost always whether they can explain why a default exists and where it bites, not whether they can recite object names.

sections.title: 1. The Kubernetes Model: Desired State, Observed State, and Control Loops
sections.content:
Most candidates open with "Kubernetes is a container orchestrator." That is true and it tells the interviewer nothing. The precise description is this: Kubernetes is a replicated, versioned datastore of *desired state* fronted by a REST API, plus a population of independent controllers that continuously compare desired state to *observed state* and take whatever action narrows the gap. Every feature in the platform — Deployments, Services, autoscaling, storage binding — is an instance of that one pattern. If you internalise the pattern, most Kubernetes behaviour becomes predictable instead of memorised.

Every object in the API has the same skeleton: `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata`, and then almost always `spec` and `status`. The division of ownership matters. `spec` is written by whoever wants something (a human, a CI pipeline, another controller) and expresses intent. `status` is written by the controller that owns the object and reports what is actually true right now. You never set `status` by hand; you never expect a controller to respect an edit you make to it. When an interviewer asks "how does a Deployment know a rollout finished," the answer starts here: the Deployment controller writes observed generation and replica counts into `status`, and `kubectl rollout status` polls that.

The loops are *level-triggered*, not edge-triggered. This is the single most important design property and it is worth saying out loud in an interview. An edge-triggered system reacts to events: "a pod was deleted, therefore create one." That system is broken by a missed message, a restart, or a network partition. A level-triggered system reacts to state: "I want 3 pods, I observe 2, therefore create 1." Events are only a hint that it is worth looking again; the decision is always recomputed from the current observed level. That is why every controller is safe to restart, why kube-controller-manager can be killed mid-rollout and resume correctly, and why reconciliation must be *idempotent* — running it twice on the same state must do the same thing as running it once.

There is a second consequence people miss: there are no cross-object transactions. Each write to the API server is an atomic update of exactly one object, and nothing more. You cannot atomically create a Deployment and its Service. You cannot assume ordering between them. Manifests applied together converge in whatever order the controllers get to them, which is why a well-written app tolerates its dependencies being briefly absent, and why `kubectl apply -f dir/` can succeed even though for two seconds the Service had no endpoints.

```
        write intent                     observe + act
user ------------------> [ API server ] <----------------- controller
                              |  ^                              |
                              v  |  watch stream                v
                           [ etcd ]  <--- only the API server writes here
```

Finally, the API is *extensible along the same axis*. A CustomResourceDefinition adds a new object kind with a spec and status; a custom controller (an "operator") runs the same reconcile loop against it. Nothing about a CRD is second-class — Postgres operators, cert-manager, and Argo CD are all just more of the same pattern. When an interviewer asks how you would automate a stateful system, the expected answer is "define the desired state as a CRD and write a level-triggered controller for it," not "write a bash script in a CronJob."

# spec is intent (you write it), status is observation (the controller writes it)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  generation: 4              # bumped by the API server on every spec change
spec:
  replicas: 3                # <- desired state
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.2
status:
  observedGeneration: 4      # <- controller has seen spec generation 4
  replicas: 3
  updatedReplicas: 3
  readyReplicas: 3
  availableReplicas: 3
  conditions:
    - type: Progressing
      status: "True"
      reason: NewReplicaSetAvailable
    - type: Available
      status: "True"

# A rollout is "done" when observedGeneration == metadata.generation
# AND updatedReplicas == replicas == availableReplicas.
# That is literally all `kubectl rollout status deploy/api` checks.

sections.title: 2. Control Plane Anatomy, and What Really Happens on `kubectl apply`
sections.content:
A cluster splits into a control plane (the brain, usually 3 or 5 replicated nodes) and worker nodes (where your containers run). The control plane components are: **etcd**, the consistent key-value store holding every object; **kube-apiserver**, the only component that reads and writes etcd and the only front door for everything else; **kube-scheduler**, which decides which node each unassigned pod belongs on; **kube-controller-manager**, a single binary hosting dozens of built-in controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job, node lifecycle, endpoints, service accounts, and more); and, on cloud clusters, **cloud-controller-manager**, which owns anything provider-specific — provisioning load balancers, attaching disks, labelling nodes with zone/region. On every node there is **kubelet**, the agent that actually runs containers, and **kube-proxy** (or an eBPF equivalent), which programs the node's packet path so Service virtual IPs work.

The critical architectural fact is the hub-and-spoke shape: **only kube-apiserver talks to etcd.** The scheduler does not. Controllers do not. Kubelet does not. Everything else is an HTTP client of the API server, which means authentication, authorization, admission control, validation, and audit logging all happen in exactly one place. It also means the API server is the availability bottleneck: when people say "the control plane is down," running pods usually keep running (kubelet has its local view and containers do not need the API server to stay alive), but nothing new can be scheduled, no rollout progresses, no Service endpoints get updated, and node failures are not acted on.

Now the classic interview question: *what happens when you run `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`?* A strong answer traces the whole path.

1. `kubectl` resolves the resource type against the API server's discovery endpoints, merges your YAML with the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation (or uses server-side apply with field ownership), and issues an HTTPS request with your credentials from kubeconfig.
2. The API server **authenticates** you (client cert, bearer token, OIDC), then **authorizes** the verb+resource+namespace via RBAC, then runs **mutating admission** (webhooks and built-ins like the ServiceAccount plugin injecting a token volume, LimitRanger inserting default requests), then **schema validation**, then **validating admission** (ResourceQuota, PodSecurity, your policy webhooks). Only then does it write the object to etcd.
3. The **Deployment controller** sees a new Deployment through its watch, computes a hash of the pod template, and creates a **ReplicaSet** with `pod-template-hash` added to its selector and labels.
4. The **ReplicaSet controller** sees a ReplicaSet with 3 desired and 0 existing pods and creates 3 Pod objects, each with an `ownerReference` back to the ReplicaSet. These pods have no `spec.nodeName`.
5. The **scheduler** watches for pods with an empty `nodeName`, filters nodes that cannot run the pod, scores the survivors, picks the best, and writes a **Binding** — effectively setting `spec.nodeName`.
6. The **kubelet** on that node sees a pod bound to itself, pulls images, asks the container runtime over CRI to create a pod sandbox (which invokes CNI to give the pod an IP and a network namespace), starts init containers, then app containers, and starts reporting container statuses back into the pod's `status`.
7. When the pod's readiness probes pass, the **EndpointSlice controller** adds the pod IP to the EndpointSlices of any matching Service, and **kube-proxy** on every node rewrites its dataplane rules so the Service ClusterIP now load-balances to that pod.

Notice that no component ever calls another component. Each one only reads and writes objects through the API server. That is the whole coordination protocol.

sections.title: 3. etcd: the Only Source of Truth (and the Only Thing You Must Back Up)
sections.content:
etcd is a strongly consistent, replicated key-value store using the Raft consensus algorithm. Kubernetes stores every object in it, serialised (by default as protobuf) under keys shaped like `/registry/<resource>/<namespace>/<name>`. Nothing else in a Kubernetes cluster is durable state. Your nodes can be rebuilt, your control plane binaries reinstalled, but if etcd is gone and you have no snapshot, the cluster's contents are gone.

Raft means writes require a **quorum** — a majority of members must acknowledge before a write commits. With 3 members you tolerate 1 failure; with 5 you tolerate 2. Even numbers buy you nothing: a 4-member cluster still needs 3 to be up, so it tolerates only 1 failure like a 3-member cluster while being slower. This is why every production guide says 3 or 5, and why an interviewer asking "why 3 masters?" is really asking whether you understand quorum. Lose quorum and the cluster goes read-only-ish and then unusable: the API server can't write, so no scheduling, no rollouts, no endpoint updates.

etcd is also latency-sensitive in a way that surprises people. Every commit is an fsync to the write-ahead log on every voting member, so **disk fsync latency directly becomes API write latency**. etcd wants low-latency local SSD/NVMe; putting etcd on network-attached storage or a noisy shared disk is a classic way to produce a cluster that "randomly" gets slow, leader-elects repeatedly, and throws `etcdserver: request timed out`. The health signals to know are `etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds` and `etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds` (99th percentile should be single-digit to low tens of milliseconds) and `etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total` (should be near-flat).

The other operational trap is space. etcd is MVCC: every write creates a new revision and old revisions are retained until *compaction* removes them, and compaction only frees space inside the file — you need *defragmentation* to return it to the filesystem. The default backend quota is 2 GiB. Cross it and etcd goes into a maintenance alarm (`NOSPACE`) and refuses writes, which reads to everyone else as "the cluster is broken." Kubernetes' API server runs compaction on an interval by default; defrag is your job (or your distro's). The usual cause of runaway growth is a controller hot-looping writes on an object, or something dumping huge objects (giant ConfigMaps, thousands of Events, oversized CRDs) into the store.

Two more etcd facts that show up in questions. First, **`resourceVersion` is the etcd revision**, which is what makes watches reliable: a client lists at revision N and then watches from N+1, so no event can be lost in the gap. It is also how optimistic concurrency works — a PUT carries the resourceVersion you read, and the API server rejects it with a 409 Conflict if someone else wrote in between. That is why controllers are written to retry on conflict rather than to lock. Second, **Secrets are stored in etcd as plaintext base64 unless you turn on encryption at rest** via an `EncryptionConfiguration` on the API server (AES-GCM, or better, a KMS provider). Anyone with the etcd data files or an etcd client cert can read every Secret in the cluster; that is why etcd peer/client TLS and disk encryption matter as much as RBAC.

# --- Backup: a snapshot is a single file and it is the whole cluster ---
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F-%H%M).db

# Verify and inspect
etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-2026-01-05-0300.db --write-out=table

# --- Health / sizing checks you should know by heart ---
etcdctl endpoint status --cluster --write-out=table   # leader, db size, raft index
etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
etcdctl alarm list                                    # NOSPACE shows up here
etcdctl defrag --cluster                              # blocks the member briefly; do one at a time

# --- Restore (rebuilds a NEW single-member data dir; stop all API servers first) ---
etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-2026-01-05-0300.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
# then point the etcd static pod at /var/lib/etcd-restored and restart it,
# and re-add the other members one at a time.

# --- What actually lives in there ---
etcdctl get /registry --prefix --keys-only | head
/registry/apiregistration.k8s.io/apiservices/v1.
/registry/configmaps/kube-system/coredns
/registry/deployments/default/api
/registry/pods/default/api-6c5f8-tn4bp

# --- Encryption at rest (API server flag: --encryption-provider-config=...) ---
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources: ["secrets"]
    providers:
      - kms:                 # preferred: key never sits on the API server host
          apiVersion: v2
          name: vault-kms
          endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
      - identity: {}         # fallback for reading pre-existing plaintext values

sections.title: 4. kube-apiserver: Authentication, Authorization, Admission, and Backpressure
sections.content:
The API server is a REST server over a versioned object model, and its request pipeline is a favourite interview topic because it is where security and policy actually live. A request travels through fixed stages, in this order:

**Authentication.** Who are you? The API server tries each configured authenticator: x509 client certificates (the CN becomes the username, `O` entries become groups — this is how kubeadm's `system:masters` admin cert works), bearer tokens including ServiceAccount JWTs, OIDC tokens from your IdP, and webhook token authenticators. The output is only a username, a UID, and a set of groups. Kubernetes has **no user objects** — there is nothing to create, and no way to "delete a user" other than revoking their credential at the source.

**Authorization.** Are you allowed to do this verb on this resource, in this namespace? Authorizers are consulted in order and the first explicit allow or deny wins; RBAC is the main one, plus the Node authorizer (which constrains what each kubelet can read to objects relevant to its own node) and optionally a webhook authorizer. Note the group `system:masters` short-circuits authorization entirely — it is a break-glass identity, not a role, and it cannot be scoped or revoked without rotating the CA or cert.

**Mutating admission.** Plugins and `MutatingAdmissionWebhook` calls may *change* the object: the ServiceAccount plugin injects the default SA and its projected token volume, LimitRanger fills in default requests/limits, a service mesh webhook injects a sidecar, your policy webhook adds labels.

**Schema validation**, then **validating admission**: `ResourceQuota` (which must run late so it counts the final object), `PodSecurity` (the built-in replacement for PodSecurityPolicy, enforcing the privileged/baseline/restricted profiles by namespace label), and `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook` / the newer CEL-based `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy`. Only after all of that does the object get persisted.

Two operational properties of the API server come up constantly. The first is **watch**. Clients don't poll; they LIST to get a consistent snapshot plus a `resourceVersion`, then WATCH from that version to receive a stream of add/update/delete events. The API server keeps an in-memory *watch cache* per resource so that thousands of watchers do not each hammer etcd. When you hear "the API server fell over during an incident," the usual mechanism is a stampede of LIST calls — a badly written controller doing `list pods` across the whole cluster every second forces the API server to serialise every pod object repeatedly, blowing up CPU and memory. The fix is to use informers (list once, watch forever) and to page/label-filter.

The second is **API Priority and Fairness**. Since it is the single front door, the API server must protect itself. APF classifies incoming requests via `FlowSchema` objects into `PriorityLevelConfiguration` buckets with their own concurrency shares and queues, so that one runaway client gets throttled with HTTP 429 (`Retry-After`) instead of starving leader election and node heartbeats. If you see 429s from the API server during a big job, this is why, and the diagnosis is `kubectl get flowschemas` plus the `apiserver_flowcontrol_*` metrics.

Finally, the API surface itself is composed. Core objects live in the legacy group (`/api/v1`), everything else in named groups (`/apis/apps/v1`, `/apis/batch/v1`). Two extension mechanisms exist: **CRDs**, where the API server itself stores and serves your new kind, and **aggregated API servers** (`APIService`), where the API server proxies a path to another server — which is how `metrics.k8s.io` works. That distinction matters in a real failure: if metrics-server is down, its APIService goes unavailable, and *discovery* degrades, which is the usual reason a namespace hangs forever in `Terminating`.
sections.code:
# ---- Who am I, and what can I do? ----
kubectl auth whoami                                  # prints username + groups
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n payments
kubectl auth can-i --list -n payments
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n payments \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:worker         # impersonation: test another identity

# ---- See the raw request pipeline decisions ----
kubectl get pods -v=8                                # full HTTP request/response trace from kubectl

# ---- Admission: enforce Pod Security by namespace label (built-in, no webhook) ----
kubectl label ns payments \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# ---- Policy without a webhook: CEL-based ValidatingAdmissionPolicy ----
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.template.spec.containers.all(c,
          has(c.resources.limits) && has(c.resources.limits.memory))
      message: "every container must set a memory limit"

# ---- Backpressure: who is being throttled? ----
kubectl get flowschemas
kubectl get prioritylevelconfigurations
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total

sections.title: 5. Controllers, Informers, Ownership, Finalizers, and Garbage Collection
sections.content:
kube-controller-manager is one process running many controllers, each an independent loop. Understanding the shared machinery explains a lot of observed behaviour.

Every controller uses an **informer**: it performs one LIST to build a local in-memory cache of the objects it cares about, then a WATCH to keep that cache current, and it re-lists periodically (the resync) as a safety net. Event handlers do not do the work; they push an object *key* (`namespace/name`) onto a rate-limited **work queue**, and worker goroutines pop keys and run `reconcile(key)`, which reads the current state from the cache and acts. Two consequences: duplicate events collapse into one reconcile (the queue dedupes keys), and reads inside a controller are from a cache that may be slightly stale. That staleness is real and is why controllers must handle "I tried to create the pod but it already exists" gracefully — a `409 AlreadyExists` is normal, not a bug.

Only one replica of each controller should act at a time, so kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler use **leader election** through a `Lease` object in `kube-system`: whoever can renew the lease acts; the others sit idle. If you ever see two rollouts fighting, suspect a broken lease or a second controller deployed by mistake.

**Ownership** is expressed with `metadata.ownerReferences`, and it does two jobs. It tells the garbage collector that when the owner is deleted, the dependents should be deleted too (this is why deleting a Deployment removes its ReplicaSets and their pods — the Deployment controller does not delete pods itself). And it tells controllers which objects are theirs. A ReplicaSet *adopts* an orphan pod that matches its selector and has no controller owner, and *releases* a pod whose labels stop matching. That is the mechanism behind the classic debugging trick: relabel a broken pod so its ReplicaSet stops owning it, the ReplicaSet immediately creates a replacement to restore the count, and you keep the broken pod alive to poke at.

Deletion has a **cascade policy**. `Foreground` sets a `foregroundDeletion` finalizer and deletes dependents first, so the owner stays visible until they are gone. `Background` (the default for most clients) deletes the owner immediately and the GC cleans up dependents afterwards. `Orphan` leaves the children behind — `kubectl delete deploy web --cascade=orphan` deletes the Deployment while leaving pods running, which is occasionally exactly what you want during a migration.

**Finalizers** are the other half and they are the most common cause of "stuck deleting" incidents. A finalizer is just a string in `metadata.finalizers`. When you delete an object that has any, the API server does not remove it; it sets `metadata.deletionTimestamp` and waits. The controller that put the finalizer there is supposed to notice the timestamp, do its cleanup (detach the disk, delete the cloud load balancer, drain the namespace), and then remove its own finalizer string. Only when the list is empty does the object actually disappear. So an object stuck `Terminating` always means the same thing: *some controller that owns a finalizer is not running, or is erroring*. A PVC hangs on `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` because a pod still mounts it. A Namespace hangs on the `kubernetes` finalizer because the namespace controller cannot enumerate or delete some resource inside it — very often a CRD whose aggregated APIService is unavailable. The correct fix is to restore the controller, not to force-remove the finalizer; stripping it leaks whatever the finalizer was supposed to clean up (real money, in the case of orphaned cloud load balancers and disks).

# --- Why is this object stuck Terminating? Always look at finalizers first. ---
kubectl get ns payments -o jsonpath='{.spec.finalizers}{"\n"}{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pvc data-0 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}{"\n"}'
# kubernetes.io/pvc-protection  -> a pod still references this PVC; find it:
kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName=="data-0") | .metadata.name'

# Namespace stuck: the usual culprit is a broken aggregated API
kubectl get apiservices | grep -v True     # any "False (ServiceNotFound/FailedDiscoveryCheck)" blocks ns deletion

# --- Ownership: see who owns a pod ---
kubectl get pod web-6c5f8-tn4bp -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences}{"\n"}'
# [{"apiVersion":"apps/v1","kind":"ReplicaSet","name":"web-6c5f8","controller":true,
#   "blockOwnerDeletion":true,"uid":"..."}]

# --- Quarantine a misbehaving pod without losing capacity ---
# ReplicaSet selector is app=web; change the label and the RS orphans this pod
kubectl label pod web-6c5f8-tn4bp app=web-quarantined --overwrite
kubectl get pods -l app=web        # RS has already created a fresh replacement

# --- Cascade choices ---
kubectl delete deploy web --cascade=foreground   # wait for pods to go first
kubectl delete deploy web --cascade=orphan       # keep the pods, drop the controller

# --- Leader election: who is actually acting? ---
kubectl -n kube-system get lease kube-controller-manager \
  -o custom-columns=HOLDER:.spec.holderIdentity,RENEWED:.spec.renewTime

sections.title: 6. kube-scheduler: Filtering, Scoring, Binding, and Preemption
sections.content:
The scheduler's job is narrow: for each pod with an empty `spec.nodeName`, choose a node. It does not create pods, it does not start containers, and it never moves a running pod. Once a pod is bound, it is bound for life — "rescheduling" in Kubernetes always means *deleting the pod and letting its controller create a new one*, which is exactly why a bare pod (one with no Deployment above it) never comes back after its node dies.

The algorithm is two phases, implemented as plugins in the **scheduling framework**. First **filter** (historically "predicates"): eliminate every node that *cannot* run the pod. Filters include `NodeResourcesFit` (does the node have enough allocatable CPU/memory/ephemeral-storage left, based on the sum of *requests* of pods already assigned there), `NodeAffinity` and `NodeName`, `TaintToleration`, `NodeUnschedulable` (cordoned nodes), `PodTopologySpread` with `DoNotSchedule`, `InterPodAffinity`, `NodePorts` (is the hostPort free), and `VolumeBinding`/`VolumeZone` (can the pod's PVCs actually be attached here). Then **score**: every surviving node gets 0–100 from each scoring plugin, weighted and summed. Defaults include `NodeResourcesFit` with the `LeastAllocated` strategy (spread load across nodes), `ImageLocality` (prefer nodes that already have the image, which saves pull time), `InterPodAffinity`, `TaintToleration`, `PodTopologySpread`, and `NodeAffinity` preferences. Highest score wins; ties broken randomly. Finally the scheduler writes a **Binding** to the pod's `binding` subresource, which sets `nodeName`.

Two things are almost always asked here. **The scheduler uses requests, not usage.** A node whose pods request 100 m CPU each but actually burn a full core will still look empty to the scheduler and will keep receiving pods until it is thrashing. Conversely a node that is 5% utilised but 100% requested is "full." Every capacity conversation in Kubernetes is really a conversation about how honest your requests are. **Limits are ignored entirely by scheduling** — they only shape runtime enforcement.

**Preemption** is the PostFilter step. If a pod is unschedulable and has a PriorityClass, the scheduler looks for a node where evicting some lower-priority pods would make the pod fit, picks the node that requires the least damage, and deletes those victims (respecting their graceful termination, and trying not to violate PodDisruptionBudgets). The victims' controllers then recreate them elsewhere, or leave them Pending. This is how you keep `system-node-critical` DaemonSets and your core services running on a saturated cluster — and how you accidentally create eviction storms if you hand out high priority classes freely. Setting `preemptionPolicy: Never` gives a pod a high scheduling *queue* position without letting it evict anybody.

Performance detail worth knowing: on large clusters the scheduler does not score every node. `percentageOfNodesToScore` makes it stop filtering once it has found a sufficient fraction of feasible nodes, trading optimality for latency. And scheduling is *one pod at a time* — there is no built-in gang/co-scheduling, which is why ML training workloads that need all N pods or none use extensions like Kueue or a custom scheduler. You can also run multiple schedulers side by side and select one per pod with `spec.schedulerName`, or hold pods out of scheduling entirely with **scheduling gates** until an external controller clears them.

When a pod stays Pending, the scheduler tells you exactly why in the pod's events, aggregated per reason: `0/9 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu, 4 node(s) had untolerated taint {gpu: true}, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector`. Read that line carefully — it accounts for every node in the cluster, and the failure category tells you whether the fix is capacity, tolerations, affinity, or volumes.

# The message format that solves 90% of Pending pods:
$ kubectl describe pod trainer-0 | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
Events:

kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: batch-job
spec:
  schedulerName: my-batch-scheduler

sections.title: 7. kubelet and the Node: CRI, Sandboxes, Node Health, and Eviction
sections.content:
kubelet is the only Kubernetes component that touches containers. It watches the API server for pods whose `spec.nodeName` equals its own node, and it runs a sync loop that makes the node's actual containers match that set. It also reads **static pod** manifests from a local directory (`/etc/kubernetes/manifests` on kubeadm clusters) and runs them without any API server involvement — which is the bootstrap trick that lets kubelet start the API server itself. Static pods appear in the API as read-only "mirror pods"; deleting the mirror pod does nothing, because kubelet owns the real one on disk.

To start a pod, kubelet talks over the **Container Runtime Interface**, a gRPC API, to containerd or CRI-O. (Docker was never spoken to via CRI directly; the `dockershim` adapter was removed in v1.24, which is what "Kubernetes dropped Docker support" actually meant — images built by Docker are OCI images and still run fine.) The runtime first creates a **pod sandbox**: a `pause` container that holds the pod's network and IPC namespaces open. The runtime invokes the **CNI** plugin, which creates a veth pair, puts one end in the sandbox's network namespace, and assigns the pod IP. Then kubelet starts init containers to completion in order, then the app containers, all joining the sandbox's namespaces — which is why containers in a pod reach each other on `localhost` and share a port number space.

kubelet's other responsibilities: pulling images (respecting `imagePullPolicy` and `imagePullSecrets`), mounting volumes (via the volume manager and CSI node plugins), running probes, executing lifecycle hooks, writing pod status back to the API, garbage collecting dead containers and unused images (driven by `imageGCHighThresholdPercent`, default 85%), and exposing container metrics that feed metrics-server. Internally, the **PLEG** (Pod Lifecycle Event Generator) polls the runtime for container state changes; a slow or wedged runtime produces the infamous `PLEG is not healthy` message and a node that flips to NotReady.

Node health is a two-part protocol. kubelet posts a **Lease** object in `kube-node-lease` roughly every 10 seconds as a cheap heartbeat, and updates the full `NodeStatus` less often. The node-lifecycle controller in kube-controller-manager watches those; if it hears nothing for the grace period (about 40 seconds by default), it marks the node `Ready=Unknown` and applies `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute`. Pods carry a default 300-second toleration for that taint (added by the DefaultTolerationSeconds admission plugin), so about five minutes later their eviction begins. **Crucially, pods on a truly dead node are only marked for deletion — they sit in `Terminating` forever, because deletion isn't final until a kubelet confirms the containers are gone, and there is no kubelet.** For a Deployment that is fine (a replacement is created). For a StatefulSet it is deliberately not: Kubernetes will not create `mysql-0` again while it may still be running and writing to a disk on a partitioned node. You resolve that by proving the node is dead — apply the `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taint (or force-delete after fencing), which lets the controllers detach volumes and recreate the pods.

Finally, **eviction**. kubelet monitors node resources and, when it crosses a threshold (defaults include `memory.available<100Mi`, `nodefs.available<10%`, `imagefs.available<15%`), sets a condition like `MemoryPressure` and starts evicting pods to reclaim. It evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods exceeding their requests, then Guaranteed pods last. Node-pressure eviction is *not* the same thing as an OOM kill: eviction is kubelet gracefully terminating a whole pod and recording a `status.reason: Evicted`, while an OOM kill is the kernel's OOM killer instantly SIGKILLing one container that exceeded its memory cgroup limit (exit code 137). A node full of `Evicted` pods usually means disk, not memory — log files and unbounded `emptyDir` are the usual offenders. Also remember `--system-reserved`/`--kube-reserved`: node `allocatable` is capacity minus those reservations minus the eviction threshold, which is why a 16 GiB node never offers a full 16 GiB to pods.

# Allocated resources: (requests, NOT usage)

sections.title: 8. Pods: Shared Namespaces, Init Containers, and Sidecars
sections.content:
A pod is not "a container." A pod is a group of containers that share a set of Linux namespaces and a lifecycle, scheduled as a unit onto one node. Concretely, all containers in a pod share the **network namespace** (one IP, one port space, they reach each other over `localhost`), the **IPC namespace**, and any volumes the pod declares. They do *not* share a mount namespace — each container keeps its own filesystem from its own image, and shares data only through explicitly mounted volumes. PID namespace sharing is off by default and opt-in via `shareProcessNamespace: true`.

The namespaces are held open by the **pause container** ("infrastructure container"), a tiny process that does nothing but sleep. It exists so that the pod's network identity survives an app container crashing and restarting: the sandbox and IP stay put while individual containers come and go. If the sandbox itself dies, the pod gets a new IP — which is the mechanical reason you must never hardcode pod IPs and must always go through a Service or DNS.

The rule for "should this be a second container in the pod or a separate pod?" is: put it in the same pod only if it must share the network namespace or a local filesystem, and must scale and be scheduled 1:1 with the main container. A log shipper reading a shared `emptyDir`, a proxy terminating TLS on localhost, a config-reloader watching a mounted ConfigMap — those belong in the pod. A cache, a database, an API you also call from elsewhere — those are separate Deployments with their own Service.

**Init containers** run sequentially, each to successful completion, before any app container starts. If one fails, the pod restarts it according to the pod's `restartPolicy`, and the pod sits in `Init:0/2` or `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` — a status people misread as the main app failing. They are the right tool for one-time setup that must not race the app: schema migrations, waiting for a dependency, fetching a secret to a shared volume, `chown`ing a mounted disk. Their resource accounting is worth knowing: the pod's effective request is `max(sum of app container requests, largest init container request)`, since init containers never run concurrently with app containers.

**Sidecar containers** were, for years, faked by putting an extra normal container in the pod, which caused two chronic problems: the sidecar could start *after* the app (races on proxies), and in a Job the sidecar never exited so the Job never completed. Kubernetes fixed this properly by adding `restartPolicy: Always` to an *init* container: such a container starts in init order, but the next init container (and eventually the app containers) start as soon as it is *started/ready* rather than waiting for it to exit, it keeps running for the pod's lifetime, it is restarted independently if it dies, and it is shut down *after* the main containers on termination, and it does not block Job completion. This landed as beta and on by default from v1.29 and has since stabilised; on older clusters you still need the workaround patterns.

Other pod-level fields that show up in interviews: `restartPolicy` (`Always` for Deployments — in fact it is the only legal value there — `OnFailure`/`Never` for Jobs; note it applies to *containers within the pod*, restarted in place on the same node, never to rescheduling the pod elsewhere); `securityContext` at pod and container level (`runAsNonRoot`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, dropping all capabilities, `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` — the baseline any security-aware interviewer expects); `hostNetwork`/`hostPID` (needed by some agents, a large blast radius otherwise); `topologySpreadConstraints`; and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    fsGroup: 10001
    seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }

  initContainers:
    # 1) classic init container: runs to completion, then the next one starts
    - name: migrate
      image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.2
      command: ["/app/migrate", "--up"]
      envFrom: [{ secretRef: { name: db-credentials } }]

    # 2) NATIVE SIDECAR: an init container with restartPolicy: Always.
    #    Starts before the app, stays up for the pod's life, stops AFTER the app,
    #    and does not prevent a Job from completing.
    - name: log-shipper
      image: fluent-bit:3.1
      restartPolicy: Always
      volumeMounts: [{ name: applogs, mountPath: /var/log/app }]

  containers:
    - name: api
      image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.2
      ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: applogs, mountPath: /var/log/app }
        - { name: tmp,     mountPath: /tmp }        # needed once root fs is read-only

  volumes:
    - name: applogs
      emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 500Mi }                # bound it, or it fills the node disk
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {}

---
# Proof that the network namespace is shared:
#   kubectl exec -it api -c log-shipper -- wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/healthz
# works even though the server runs in the OTHER container.

sections.title: 9. Pod Lifecycle and Graceful Termination: the Race Everyone Ships With
sections.content:
Pod `status.phase` is coarse — `Pending`, `Running`, `Succeeded`, `Failed`, `Unknown` — and it is not where the detail lives. The useful signal is in `status.conditions` (`PodScheduled`, `Initialized`, `ContainersReady`, `Ready`) and `status.containerStatuses[].state`, which is one of `waiting` (with a reason like `ContainerCreating`, `ImagePullBackOff`, `CrashLoopBackOff`), `running`, or `terminated` (with an exit code and reason such as `OOMKilled`, `Error`, `Completed`). "Pod is Running" tells you the sandbox exists and at least one container started; it says nothing about readiness.

Startup order: sandbox created and IP assigned → init containers in order → native sidecars started → app containers started (in list order, but Kubernetes does not wait for one to be ready before starting the next, so ordering between app containers is not a guarantee you can build on) → `postStart` hooks fire asynchronously → startup/readiness probes begin gating traffic.

Termination is where the interesting bug lives, and it is one of the highest-signal questions you can be asked. When a pod is deleted (by you, by a rollout, by an eviction, by node drain), this happens:

1. The API server sets `deletionTimestamp` and the pod's grace period begins. The pod is now `Terminating`.
2. **In parallel**, two independent things start: (a) the EndpointSlice controller removes the pod from the Service's endpoints, which then has to propagate to kube-proxy on every node, or to every Ingress controller and mesh sidecar holding its own endpoint list; and (b) kubelet runs the container's `preStop` hook and then sends **SIGTERM** to PID 1 of each container.
3. When the grace period (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, default 30s, and the `preStop` hook runs *inside* that budget) expires, kubelet sends **SIGKILL**.
4. Once the runtime confirms the containers are gone, kubelet tells the API server, and the pod object is finally removed.

The race is in step 2. Nothing sequences endpoint removal *before* SIGTERM. Your app may begin shutting down while kube-proxy rules on other nodes still point at it, so requests arrive at a socket that is closing → connection refused, RST, or 502s at the ingress, precisely during every deploy. The standard, correct mitigation is a `preStop` hook that simply sleeps a few seconds: the container keeps serving normally during the sleep, giving endpoint removal time to propagate, and only then does SIGTERM arrive. Five to fifteen seconds is typical; it must be comfortably less than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, because the grace clock covers both the hook and the shutdown.

The second half is your application's job: on SIGTERM it must stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close upstream connections cleanly, and exit. Two classic failures here. First, **PID 1 signal semantics**: if your container's entrypoint is a shell (`CMD npm start`, or `sh -c "..."`), the shell is PID 1, and it typically does not forward SIGTERM to your app — so nothing happens for 30 seconds and then everything is SIGKILLed, dropping every in-flight request. Use exec form (`CMD ["node","server.js"]`), or a tiny init like `tini`, and make sure your framework installs a signal handler. Second, **long-lived connections**: HTTP keep-alive, gRPC channels, and WebSockets don't care that endpoints changed, because the client already has an open TCP connection to that pod IP. Kubernetes has no mechanism to steer those; the server must send `GOAWAY` (gRPC/HTTP-2) or `Connection: close` and let clients reconnect through the Service.

Related: `kubectl drain` uses the **Eviction API**, not a raw delete, which means it respects PodDisruptionBudgets and will block rather than take your last healthy replica. Nothing respects PDBs when the kernel panics — PDBs cover *voluntary* disruptions only.
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60      # must exceed preStop sleep + real drain time
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.2
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                # Keep serving while endpoint removal propagates to every kube-proxy /
                # ingress controller. THEN let SIGTERM arrive.
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 2

---
# PodDisruptionBudget: drains and node upgrades must leave this much capacity
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  minAvailable: 80%          # or maxUnavailable: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }

# Draining a node for maintenance (this BLOCKS on the PDB above -- that is the point)
kubectl cordon node4                                  # stop new pods landing here
kubectl drain node4 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=15m
# ... maintenance ...
kubectl uncordon node4

# Watch a termination in real time
kubectl get pod api-xxxx -w
kubectl get pod api-xxxx -o jsonpath='{.metadata.deletionTimestamp} {.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}{"\n"}'

# Dockerfile side: exec form so your process is PID 1 and actually receives SIGTERM
# BAD :  CMD npm start                 -> /bin/sh is PID 1, swallows SIGTERM
# GOOD:  CMD ["node", "server.js"]
# GOOD:  ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini","--"]  +  CMD ["node","server.js"]

sections.title: 10. ReplicaSets and Deployments: the Three-Layer Stack
sections.content:
There are three objects and each has exactly one job. A **Pod** is a running unit with no self-healing — delete it and nothing brings it back. A **ReplicaSet** keeps N pods matching a label selector alive; that is its entire purpose. A **Deployment** manages ReplicaSets to give you versioned, controlled transitions between pod templates. You essentially never create a ReplicaSet by hand; you create a Deployment and it creates ReplicaSets for you.

The mechanism that makes this work is the `pod-template-hash`. When the Deployment controller reconciles, it hashes the pod template and looks for a ReplicaSet whose template matches. If none exists it creates one named `<deployment>-<hash>`, and it injects `pod-template-hash: <hash>` into *both* the ReplicaSet's selector and its pod template labels. That extra label is what keeps two ReplicaSets from stealing each other's pods during a rollout — old and new both select `app=api`, but their hashes differ, so each owns only its own generation. This is also why the Deployment's `.spec.selector` is immutable in `apps/v1`: changing it would orphan every existing ReplicaSet.

ReplicaSet reconciliation is a simple diff: count pods matching the selector that are not terminating, compare to `spec.replicas`, create or delete the difference. When it must delete, it does not pick randomly — it prefers pods that are unscheduled, then Pending over Running, then not-ready over ready, then pods on nodes with more replicas of the same set, then the youngest (by ready time) — so scaling down tends to remove the least valuable pod. Adoption matters too: a ReplicaSet will *adopt* any pod matching its selector that has no controller owner. Create a bare pod with `app=api` in the same namespace and the ReplicaSet may count it towards its replica total and delete one of its own; label carelessness has caused real outages this way. Always use selectors specific enough to be unambiguous.

Labels and selectors are the universal join key in Kubernetes and worth precision. Selectors come in two flavours: equality-based (`app=api,tier=backend`, all terms ANDed) and set-based (`env in (staging,prod)`, `!canary`, `tier notin (db)`). Deployments/ReplicaSets/Services/NetworkPolicies all select pods this way, and there is no referential integrity — a Service whose selector matches nothing is perfectly legal and simply has no endpoints. `kubectl get endpointslices` returning nothing is therefore the single most useful check when "the Service doesn't work."

A last distinction interviewers use as a filter: **`replicas` is not high availability.** Three replicas can all land on one node, one rack, or one AZ. Getting real availability requires `topologySpreadConstraints` (or anti-affinity), a PodDisruptionBudget so drains and upgrades can't take them all at once, and requests set honestly enough that the scheduler's placement means something. And do not use `kubectl scale` or edit `replicas` in a cluster where an HPA also manages that Deployment — they will fight, with the HPA winning on its next 15-second sync.

sections.title: 11. Rolling Updates, Rollbacks, and Safer Release Strategies
sections.content:
A rolling update is the Deployment controller moving pods from the old ReplicaSet to a new one, a few at a time, bounded by two knobs. `maxUnavailable` (default 25%) is how far below `replicas` the *available* count may drop. `maxSurge` (default 25%) is how far above `replicas` the total pod count may go. With 10 replicas and the defaults, the controller may run up to 13 pods at once and must keep at least 8 available (percentages round down for unavailable, up for surge). Each step: scale the new RS up within the surge budget, wait for new pods to become **Available**, scale the old RS down within the unavailable budget, repeat.

"Available" is the load-bearing word. A pod is Ready when its readiness probe passes, and Available when it has been Ready continuously for `minReadySeconds` (default 0). **If you have no readiness probe, pods are considered Ready the instant their containers start, so the rollout will happily replace all your healthy old pods with new ones that are still booting — and you get an outage from a rollout that "worked."** A readiness probe plus a nonzero `minReadySeconds` (10–30s for a service with a warm-up) is what makes a rolling update actually safe. This is the highest-value thing to say when asked "how do you get zero-downtime deploys."

If the new pods never become Available, the rollout does not automatically undo itself. It stalls, and after `progressDeadlineSeconds` (default 600) the Deployment gets a `Progressing=False` condition with reason `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. `kubectl rollout status` exits non-zero at that point, which is how CI detects a bad deploy. The safety property to appreciate: the old ReplicaSet is only scaled down as new pods become available, so a totally broken image (CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff) burns your surge budget and stops — most of your old pods are still serving. A *partially* broken release, one that passes readiness but returns 500s, will roll all the way out. Probes only catch what they measure.

Rollback works because old ReplicaSets are kept, scaled to zero, up to `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10). `kubectl rollout undo` just repoints the Deployment's template at a previous revision's template, which causes the controller to scale that old ReplicaSet back up — so a rollback is itself a rolling update, with the same safety properties, and typically much faster because the images are already on the nodes. Note `kubectl rollout history` shows a useful CHANGE-CAUSE only if you set the `kubernetes.io/change-cause` annotation. A rollback of *code* is not a rollback of *state*: if the new version ran a non-backwards-compatible database migration, undoing the Deployment gives you old code against a new schema. Expand/contract migrations (add column, deploy code that tolerates both, backfill, then remove) exist for exactly this.

`strategy.type: Recreate` is the other built-in: kill everything, then start the new version. It causes downtime and is correct only when two versions genuinely cannot coexist — a single-writer process, an exclusive `ReadWriteOnce` volume, an incompatible schema lock.

Beyond that, Kubernetes has no native canary or blue/green primitive; you build it. **Blue/green** = two Deployments and one Service whose selector you flip (instant cutover, instant rollback, double the capacity cost, and open connections to blue are not migrated). **Poor-man's canary** = two Deployments sharing the Service selector with different replica counts, so traffic split is proportional to pod count (9 stable + 1 canary ≈ 10%) — coarse, but zero extra machinery. **Real canary** = an ingress controller or service mesh doing weighted routing by header or percentage, driven by an operator like Argo Rollouts or Flagger that watches your error-rate and latency SLIs and promotes or aborts automatically. In an interview, name the three, say what each costs, and mention that whichever you pick must be paired with an automatic abort signal, because a human watching a dashboard is not a rollback strategy.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "bump api to 1.8.3 (fixes CVE-2026-1234)"
spec:
  replicas: 10
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300      # fail the rollout in 5 min, not 10
  minReadySeconds: 15               # be Ready for 15s before counting as Available
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 2                   # at most 12 pods total
      maxUnavailable: 0             # never dip below 10 available -> safest, needs headroom
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.3
          readinessProbe:                    # WITHOUT THIS, maxUnavailable is meaningless
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5

---
# Driving and observing rollouts
kubectl set image deploy/api api=registry.example.com/api:1.8.3
kubectl annotate deploy/api kubernetes.io/change-cause="api 1.8.3" --overwrite

kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=5m   # exit code != 0 => CI fails the deploy
kubectl rollout pause  deploy/api                # freeze mid-rollout to inspect the canary pods
kubectl rollout resume deploy/api
kubectl rollout history deploy/api
kubectl rollout history deploy/api --revision=7
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api                  # previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api --to-revision=7
kubectl rollout restart deploy/api               # re-roll with the SAME image
# (restart works by stamping template annotation kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt,
#  which changes the pod-template-hash and creates a new ReplicaSet)

# Why is my rollout stuck?
kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'
# Progressing=False ProgressDeadlineExceeded  -> new pods never became Available
kubectl describe rs $(kubectl get rs -l app=api --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -o name | tail -1)

sections.title: 12. Services and kube-proxy: How a ClusterIP Actually Works
sections.content:
Pods are mortal and their IPs change on every restart, so you need a stable address with load balancing in front of a changing set of backends. That is a Service. The important insight, and the one candidates most often miss: **a ClusterIP is not an address that anything listens on.** There is no proxy process bound to it, no interface holding it. It is a virtual IP from the service CIDR that exists purely as a rule in every node's packet-processing path. When a pod connects to `10.96.14.7:80`, the node's kernel rewrites the destination to a real pod IP (DNAT) before the packet leaves; the reply is un-NATed on the way back. Nothing ever "arrives at" the ClusterIP. That is why you cannot ping most ClusterIPs (no ICMP rule exists) and why `tcpdump` on a node never shows the Service IP on the wire between nodes.

The rules are written by **kube-proxy**, a DaemonSet on every node that watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs the dataplane. In the default **iptables** mode, it writes chains under `KUBE-SERVICES` that match the service VIP+port and jump to one `KUBE-SEP-*` chain per endpoint, using the `statistic random probability` module to pick uniformly. It is stable and simple but rule evaluation is a linear list, and a full resync of tens of thousands of rules on every endpoint change becomes a real cost on very large clusters. **IPVS** mode uses the kernel's in-kernel L4 load balancer with hash-based lookup, so it scales better and supports algorithms beyond random (`rr`, `lc`, `sh`). A newer **nftables** mode (beta from v1.31) gives iptables-mode semantics with much better update and lookup performance and is where things are heading. Some CNIs (Cilium in particular) replace kube-proxy altogether with eBPF programs at the socket/XDP layer.

Backends are tracked in **EndpointSlice** objects (the modern replacement for the single `Endpoints` object, which had to be rewritten in full on every change — a 5,000-endpoint Service produced a megabyte-scale write per pod flap). Slices hold up to 100 endpoints each by default, each with `conditions.ready`, `serving`, and `terminating`, plus topology hints. The endpoint controller adds a pod's IP only when the pod is Ready; that is the whole readiness-probe-to-traffic mechanism.

Service types stack on one another. **ClusterIP** is the base: reachable only inside the cluster. **NodePort** is a ClusterIP plus a port (default range 30000–32767) opened on *every* node, which forwards to the Service. **LoadBalancer** is a NodePort plus a cloud load balancer provisioned by the cloud-controller-manager, targeting those node ports (or, with modern cloud CNIs, pod IPs directly). **ExternalName** is different in kind: no proxying at all, just a CNAME returned by CoreDNS. And a Service with `clusterIP: None` is **headless**: no VIP, no kube-proxy rules; DNS returns the pod IPs directly, which is what StatefulSets and clients that do their own load balancing (gRPC, most database drivers) want.

Two fields cause most real-world surprises. `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` (default) lets any node accept external traffic and forward it to a pod on any node — even spread, but a second hop and **the client source IP is SNATed away**, so your access logs show node IPs. `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` drops traffic that arrives at a node with no local pod, preserving the client IP; the cloud LB stops sending to those nodes because they fail the `healthCheckNodePort` check. Local preserves source IP and removes a hop, but load is now proportional to *pods per node*, so you need reasonably even spread. Separately, remember that a Service load-balances **per new TCP connection**, not per request — an HTTP/2 or gRPC client that opens one long-lived connection will pin to one pod forever. The fixes are a headless Service with client-side load balancing, a proxy/mesh that does L7 balancing, or periodic connection recycling (`MAX_CONNECTION_AGE`).
