sections.title: 13. Cluster DNS: CoreDNS, Search Paths, and the ndots Trap
sections.content:
Service discovery in Kubernetes is DNS. **CoreDNS** runs as a Deployment in `kube-system` behind a ClusterIP Service (conventionally `10.96.0.10`), and kubelet writes that address into every pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`. CoreDNS watches Services and EndpointSlices through the API server and answers from memory — it is not reading a zone file, and there is no zone transfer or TTL-driven refresh from an authoritative upstream.

The naming scheme is fully deterministic: a Service gets `<service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`, normally `svc.cluster.local`. For a normal ClusterIP Service the A/AAAA record is the *virtual IP*. For a headless Service, the same name returns the **set of ready pod IPs**, and each pod additionally gets `<pod-hostname>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` — which for a StatefulSet means `mysql-0.mysql.prod.svc.cluster.local`, the stable per-replica identity that clustered databases depend on. Named ports also get SRV records (`_http._tcp.<service>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`).

Now the performance trap that every Kubernetes operator eventually meets. kubelet writes a **search path** into the pod's resolv.conf — `<ns>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local` plus the node's own domains — and sets **`options ndots:5`**. The resolver rule is: if a name contains fewer than `ndots` dots, try each search-domain suffix *first*, and only then try the name as absolute. `api.example.com` has two dots, which is fewer than five, so a pod resolving it issues `api.example.com.prod.svc.cluster.local`, `api.example.com.svc.cluster.local`, `api.example.com.cluster.local`, then the node's suffixes, and only finally `api.example.com.` — potentially 8–10 queries (A and AAAA for each) for one external lookup. At scale this melts CoreDNS and shows up as random multi-second latency spikes on outbound calls. The fixes, in order of preference: use a fully qualified name with a trailing dot (`api.example.com.`) so the search path is skipped; lower `ndots` for that pod via `dnsConfig`; enable NodeLocal DNSCache (a per-node DNS cache DaemonSet that also converts UDP to TCP upstream and removes a lot of conntrack pressure); and scale CoreDNS with its `cache` and `autopath` plugins tuned.

Other things worth knowing: DNS resolution respects readiness — unready pods are excluded from headless records unless the Service sets `publishNotReadyAddresses: true`, which clustered systems sometimes need during bootstrap so members can find each other before any of them is "ready." `dnsPolicy` on the pod matters: `ClusterFirst` is the default; `Default` means "inherit the node's resolv.conf" (i.e. no cluster DNS at all); `None` plus an explicit `dnsConfig` gives you full control; and pods with `hostNetwork: true` get `Default` unless you explicitly set `ClusterFirstWithHostNet`, which is a very common cause of "my host-network agent can't resolve Kubernetes services."

When something can't be reached, DNS is the first thing to isolate, because a name failure and a connectivity failure look identical to an application. Check resolution and connectivity separately, from inside a pod in the same namespace as the caller.
sections.code:
# What every pod gets
$ kubectl exec -it api-xxxx -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.96.0.10
search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local ec2.internal
options ndots:5

# The cost of ndots:5 on an EXTERNAL name (watch the failed attempts)
$ kubectl exec -it api-xxxx -- sh -c 'dig +search +short api.example.com | head'
# vs the cheap version -- note the trailing dot (fully qualified, skips the search path)
$ kubectl exec -it api-xxxx -- sh -c 'dig +short api.example.com.'

---
# Per-pod fix for chatty external DNS
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: egress-heavy }
spec:
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - { name: ndots, value: "2" }
      - { name: single-request-open }     # send A and AAAA in parallel on one socket
  containers: [{ name: app, image: app:1.0 }]

---
# Host-network pods MUST opt in to cluster DNS
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet      # otherwise they use the node's resolv.conf

---
# Headless Service + StatefulSet gives stable per-pod names
$ kubectl exec -it client -- nslookup mysql.prod.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.244.1.7      # mysql-0
Address: 10.244.2.9      # mysql-1
$ kubectl exec -it client -- nslookup mysql-0.mysql.prod.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.244.1.7

# Triage
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy coredns
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=100
kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml       # the Corefile: cache, forward, autopath
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep coredns_dns_request_duration   # (scrape CoreDNS directly)

sections.title: 14. Ingress and the Gateway API: L7 Entry into the Cluster
sections.content:
A `LoadBalancer` Service gives you one cloud load balancer per service, which is fine for two services and absurd for two hundred — you pay for each, and you get no HTTP-level features. **Ingress** solves that: one entry point that routes HTTP(S) by host and path to many backend Services, terminating TLS centrally.

The point candidates most often get wrong: **the Ingress object does nothing on its own.** It is a piece of configuration with no built-in implementation. You must install an **ingress controller** — ingress-nginx, HAProxy, Traefik, Envoy-based controllers, or a cloud one like AWS Load Balancer Controller or GKE's — which is itself a Deployment (usually fronted by a single `LoadBalancer` Service) that watches Ingress objects and reconfigures its own proxy. Create an Ingress in a cluster with no controller and you get a permanently blank `ADDRESS` field and no error, which is exactly the symptom people spend an hour on.

Which controller handles which Ingress is decided by `spec.ingressClassName` referencing an `IngressClass` object (the old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation is deprecated). One IngressClass may be marked default. Routing rules match a `host` and a set of paths, each with a required `pathType`: `Prefix` matches whole path *segments* (`/api` matches `/api/v1` but not `/apifoo`), `Exact` is literal, and `ImplementationSpecific` hands interpretation to the controller — which is what lets ingress-nginx accept regexes. TLS is a list of hosts plus a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls` containing `tls.crt`/`tls.key`, typically issued automatically by cert-manager, which watches Ingresses and runs ACME on your behalf.

Note the traffic path with an ingress controller: client → cloud LB → controller pod → **directly to a backend pod IP**. Most controllers read EndpointSlices themselves and bypass the Service ClusterIP entirely, which is why they can do their own load-balancing algorithms, retries, and sticky sessions — and also why an ingress controller keeps its own view of endpoints that must converge during a rollout (another reason for the `preStop` sleep).

The honest weakness of Ingress is that the core spec covers almost nothing beyond host/path routing and TLS, so every real feature — rewrites, timeouts, rate limits, canary weights, auth, CORS, mTLS to the backend — lives in **controller-specific annotations**. Your manifests become non-portable, and the annotations are stringly typed with no validation. That is precisely the problem the **Gateway API** was designed to fix. It is a set of CRDs (`GatewayClass`, `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`, `GRPCRoute`, plus `TLSRoute`/`TCPRoute`) that reached v1.0/GA for the core HTTP set, with three properties Ingress lacks: routing features like header matching, traffic splitting by weight, and request mirroring are **first-class typed fields**, not annotations; the model is **role-oriented**, so a platform team owns the `Gateway` (listeners, certs, IPs) while app teams own `HTTPRoute` objects in their own namespaces, with explicit cross-namespace attachment permission (`ReferenceGrant`); and it is expressible enough that service meshes and ingress implementations can share one API. Gateway API is the direction of travel; Ingress is frozen in maintenance mode but is not going away. In an interview, being able to say *why* Gateway API exists — annotation sprawl and the lack of a role/tenancy model — is worth more than reciting its object names.
sections.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "20m"     # controller-specific: not portable
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [shop.example.com]
      secretName: shop-tls                                  # type: kubernetes.io/tls
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix        # segment-aware: /api/v1 yes, /apifoo no
            backend:
              service:
                name: api
                port: { number: 80 }
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port: { name: http }

---
# Gateway API: same job, typed fields, split ownership
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: { name: edge, namespace: infra }      # owned by the platform team
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: "*.example.com"
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs: [{ name: wildcard-example-tls }]
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces: { from: Selector, selector: { matchLabels: { gateway-access: "true" } } }
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: { name: api, namespace: payments }    # owned by the app team
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: edge, namespace: infra }]
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /api }
          headers: [{ name: x-canary, value: "true" }]      # header matching is FIRST-CLASS
      backendRefs: [{ name: api-canary, port: 80 }]
    - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /api } }]
      backendRefs:                                          # weighted split, no annotations
        - { name: api,        port: 80, weight: 95 }
        - { name: api-canary, port: 80, weight: 5 }

# "My Ingress has no ADDRESS":
kubectl get ingressclass                 # is a controller even installed?
kubectl -n ingress-nginx get pods,svc
kubectl describe ing shop                # events from the controller land here

sections.title: 15. ConfigMaps and Secrets: Projection, Propagation, and Real Security
sections.content:
ConfigMaps and Secrets both hold key/value data and both exist to keep configuration out of images, so the same image artifact can run in dev, staging, and prod. Mechanically they are near-identical objects — Secrets store `data` base64-encoded and are handled a bit more carefully by the platform (mounted from tmpfs, redacted in some outputs, separately encryptable at rest) but **base64 is encoding, not encryption**. Anyone who can `get` the Secret, or read etcd, sees the value. Saying that plainly in an interview is a positive signal; treating Secrets as inherently safe is a negative one.

There are two ways to project them into a pod and the difference matters enormously.

**As environment variables** (`env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` / `secretKeyRef`, or `envFrom`): values are read once, at container start, and baked into the process environment. **They never update.** Change the ConfigMap and the running pod keeps the old value forever. Environment variables also leak easily — they show up in `/proc/<pid>/environ`, in crash dumps, in child processes, and in `kubectl describe pod` for the non-secret case. And if a referenced key is missing, the pod won't start (`CreateContainerConfigError`), which is a frequent "why is my pod stuck" answer.

**As a volume**: kubelet writes the keys as files into a directory and *does* keep them updated. The update is atomic — kubelet writes a new timestamped directory and swaps a `..data` symlink — so a reader never sees a half-written file. Propagation is not instant: it takes up to the kubelet sync period (about a minute by default) plus cache delay. The critical exception: **a `subPath` mount does not receive updates**, because it bypasses the symlink indirection. That trips up everyone who mounts a single file into `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` with `subPath` and wonders why reloads never pick up changes; the workaround is to mount the whole directory, or use a `projected` volume, or accept restart-on-change.

Even with volume updates, your *application* must reload the file — most do not. So in practice the industry converged on **treating config as immutable and rolling the pods**: name ConfigMaps with a content hash (`app-config-7f3a9c`), reference that name, and let a changed name produce a new pod template and therefore a normal, observable, rollback-able rolling update. Helm's `checksum/config` annotation and Kustomize's `configMapGenerator` hash suffixes do exactly this. It converts an invisible, staggered, unversioned config change into a deploy — which is what you want when a bad config value is as capable of causing an outage as bad code. Setting `immutable: true` on a ConfigMap/Secret is complementary: it forbids updates and lets kubelet stop watching the object, which meaningfully reduces API server load in large clusters.

Real Secret hygiene, in the order interviewers expect to hear it: enable **encryption at rest** with a KMS provider so etcd doesn't hold plaintext; lock down RBAC, because `get secrets` in a namespace is effectively "read every credential in that namespace," and `create pod` in a namespace is close to it (you can mount any ServiceAccount there and read its token); prefer **short-lived, workload-identity-based credentials** over static ones — projected ServiceAccount tokens with an audience and expiry, IRSA/Workload Identity for cloud APIs, Vault or the Secrets Store CSI driver for dynamic database credentials — because a secret that rotates every hour is worth far more than one that is encrypted but eternal; and never commit plaintext secrets to Git (Sealed Secrets or SOPS if you must do GitOps with secrets in the repo, External Secrets Operator if you'd rather sync from a real secret manager). Note also that both objects are capped around 1 MiB, so they are not a distribution channel for large files, and that changing a Secret does not restart consumers — the same reload problem applies.
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: api-config-7f3a9c       # content hash in the name => changing config = new rollout
  namespace: payments
immutable: true                 # cannot be edited; kubelet stops watching it (less API load)
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  app.yaml: |
    server:
      timeout: 30s
      maxConnections: 500
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api, namespace: payments }
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "7f3a9c"        # forces a rolling update when config changes
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.3
          env:
            - name: LOG_LEVEL                      # snapshot at start; never updates
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef: { name: api-config-7f3a9c, key: LOG_LEVEL }
            - name: DB_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: db-credentials, key: password }
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app            # whole dir -> live updates via ..data symlink swap
            # - name: config
            #   mountPath: /etc/app/app.yaml
            #   subPath: app.yaml            # <- DO NOT: subPath mounts never update
            - name: sa-token
              mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap: { name: api-config-7f3a9c }
        - name: sa-token
          projected:
            sources:
              - serviceAccountToken:         # short-lived, audience-bound, auto-refreshed
                  path: vault-token
                  audience: vault
                  expirationSeconds: 3600

---
# Inspecting (note: `get -o yaml` shows base64, not plaintext)
kubectl create secret generic db-credentials \
  --from-literal=password='s3cr3t' --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'   # check for last-applied leaks!

# Who can read secrets in this namespace? (this is your real threat model)
kubectl auth can-i --list -n payments --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:default | grep secrets

sections.title: 16. Namespaces, ResourceQuota, and LimitRange
sections.content:
A namespace is a scope for names, nothing more and nothing less. Object names must be unique within a namespace for a given kind, and the namespace becomes part of the DNS name (`api.payments.svc.cluster.local`). Not everything is namespaced: Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, IngressClasses, PriorityClasses, and CRD definitions themselves are cluster-scoped. `kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false` lists them, which is a genuinely useful command to know.

The essential point in an interview: **a namespace is not a security boundary by itself.** By default, pods in namespace A can open TCP connections to pod IPs in namespace B — there is nothing between them. Namespaces give you a place to *attach* boundaries; the boundaries themselves are separate objects. To get an actual boundary you compose: RBAC (Roles and RoleBindings scoped to the namespace) for API access, **NetworkPolicy** for pod-to-pod traffic, **ResourceQuota** so one tenant can't starve the cluster, **LimitRange** so pods can't request absurd amounts, Pod Security admission labels so nobody runs privileged containers, and separate ServiceAccounts. If a candidate says "we isolate tenants with namespaces," the follow-up is always "how?" — and the expected answer is that list. For genuinely hostile multi-tenancy (running untrusted code), even that is not enough: the shared kernel is the boundary, and you need separate clusters, or at minimum sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata) and dedicated node pools.

**ResourceQuota** is a namespace-scoped cap enforced at admission time. It can limit the sum of `requests.cpu`, `requests.memory`, `limits.cpu`, `limits.memory`, `requests.storage`, per-StorageClass PVC storage, and object counts (`pods`, `services`, `services.loadbalancers`, `count/deployments.apps`, and so on — capping LoadBalancer Services is a nice trick for cloud cost control). Two behaviours you must know because they cause confusing failures. First, quotas are checked when the *pod* is created, and the rejection surfaces on the **ReplicaSet**, not on your Deployment — so a Deployment that says `3` sits at `1/3` with no obvious error until you `kubectl describe rs` and see `exceeded quota`. Second, **if a quota constrains `requests.cpu` or `limits.memory`, then every pod in that namespace must specify that field**, or its creation is rejected outright. That is why a quota deployed into an existing namespace can instantly break every subsequent rollout of workloads that never set resources. The intended pairing is a LimitRange supplying defaults.

**LimitRange** is the other half: a namespace-level policy that applies at admission to individual pods/containers/PVCs. `default` supplies a limit when none is given, `defaultRequest` supplies a request, `min`/`max` reject anything outside a band, and `maxLimitRequestRatio` caps how far a limit may exceed its request (which stops people from writing `requests: 10m, limits: 8` and creating a node full of pods that all believe they can burst to 8 cores). LimitRange defaults are *mutating* — they rewrite the pod spec at admission, which is why `kubectl get pod -o yaml` shows resources you never wrote.

Finally, namespace deletion. Deleting a namespace triggers the namespace controller to enumerate every resource type in it and delete them; only then does it remove the `kubernetes` finalizer and the namespace object. If any API group is unavailable — a webhook that is down, an aggregated APIService whose backing service is gone, a CRD whose operator was deleted before its custom resources — the controller cannot complete the enumeration and the namespace sits in `Terminating` indefinitely. Look at `.status.conditions` on the namespace; it names the failing group. Force-removing the finalizer "works" only in the sense that it hides the object and leaks its contents.
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: { name: team-quota, namespace: payments }
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "40"
    requests.memory: 80Gi
    limits.cpu: "80"
    limits.memory: 160Gi
    requests.storage: 2Ti
    persistentvolumeclaims: "30"
    pods: "150"
    services.loadbalancers: "2"          # cloud cost guardrail
    count/deployments.apps: "50"
---
# Scoped quota: batch work (low priority) gets its own smaller budget
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: { name: batch-quota, namespace: payments }
spec:
  hard: { requests.cpu: "10", requests.memory: 20Gi }
  scopeSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - { scopeName: PriorityClass, operator: In, values: ["batch-low"] }
---
# Without this, the quota above makes every pod that omits resources UNSCHEDULABLE
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: { name: defaults, namespace: payments }
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:            { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }   # -> limits if unset
      defaultRequest:     { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }   # -> requests if unset
      min:                { cpu: 10m,  memory: 32Mi }
      max:                { cpu: "8",  memory: 32Gi }
      maxLimitRequestRatio: { cpu: "10" }                # stop 10m -> 8 core burst claims
    - type: PersistentVolumeClaim
      min: { storage: 1Gi }
      max: { storage: 500Gi }

# ---- Operating with quotas ----
kubectl describe quota -n payments          # USED vs HARD, per resource
kubectl get quota -n payments -o yaml

# "My Deployment says 3/3 desired but only 1 pod exists" -> look at the ReplicaSet, not the Deployment
kubectl describe rs -n payments api-7d9fbb6c84 | tail -5
#   Warning  FailedCreate  ... pods "api-7d9..." is forbidden:
#   exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: requests.cpu=2, used: requests.cpu=39, limited: requests.cpu=40

# Namespace stuck Terminating -> the condition names the broken API group
kubectl get ns payments -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}: {.message}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false | head

sections.title: 17. Requests, Limits, cgroups, QoS, and Why Your Pod Was Killed
sections.content:
This is the topic that separates people who have operated Kubernetes from people who have read about it, so expect it to be probed hard.

A **request** is a scheduling contract: "reserve this much for me on a node." The scheduler sums requests of pods already assigned to a node and will not place a pod whose requests do not fit in `allocatable`. A **limit** is a runtime cap enforced by the kernel through cgroups. They are enforced by completely different subsystems at completely different times, and CPU and memory behave completely differently.

**CPU is compressible.** The request becomes a cgroup weight (`cpu.shares` on cgroup v1, `cpu.weight` on v2), which only matters when the CPU is contended: a container requesting 500m gets twice the share of one requesting 250m, but if the CPU is idle, either can use the whole machine. The limit becomes CFS bandwidth: a quota of N microseconds per 100 ms period (`cpu.cfs_quota_us`/`cpu.max`). When the container exhausts its quota within a period, **every thread is frozen until the next period begins** — this is CPU **throttling**, and it is a latency event, not an error, so it is invisible unless you watch `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total`. It bites hardest for multi-threaded runtimes: a Go or JVM process with 8 OS threads and a 1-core limit burns its 100 ms of quota in 12.5 ms of wall time and then sits frozen for 87 ms. This is why "we added CPU limits and p99 got worse" is a real and common experience, and why a defensible position in a modern interview is: **always set CPU requests, be very deliberate about CPU limits** — often omit them for latency-sensitive services (letting the request-based weight handle contention fairly) and use them where predictability or hard tenancy isolation matters more than tail latency.

**Memory is incompressible.** The request is only used for scheduling; the limit becomes `memory.max`. Exceed it and the kernel's OOM killer terminates the offending process immediately — no warning, no signal to handle, exit code **137** (128 + SIGKILL). kubelet reports `OOMKilled` in the container's `lastState.terminated.reason`, the container restarts per `restartPolicy`, and repeated occurrences produce CrashLoopBackOff. A subtlety worth mentioning: cgroup accounting includes page cache attributable to the cgroup, so a process doing heavy file I/O can be OOM-killed even when its heap is modest. And **container memory limits are not automatically the runtime's heap ceiling** — modern JVMs are container-aware and use `MaxRAMPercentage`, but Node's old default heap, many Python workers, and anything computing "available memory" from `/proc/meminfo` will happily size themselves to the *node's* RAM and get killed. Setting the runtime's own memory ceiling to a fraction of the container limit (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`, `GOMEMLIMIT`, `--max-old-space-size`) is the fix.

From requests and limits Kubernetes derives a **QoS class**, and this is a very common question. **Guaranteed**: *every* container in the pod sets both requests and limits for both CPU and memory, and request == limit for each. **Burstable**: at least one request is set, but it isn't Guaranteed. **BestEffort**: no requests or limits anywhere in the pod. QoS drives two things: the OOM score adjustment (Guaranteed gets roughly -997, BestEffort 1000, Burstable something in between, so under *node-level* memory exhaustion the kernel eats BestEffort pods first) and kubelet's node-pressure **eviction** order (BestEffort first, then Burstable pods that are over their requests, then Guaranteed). Guaranteed pods also unlock CPU pinning under the static CPU manager policy (integer CPU limits get exclusive cores, avoiding cache/NUMA thrash) — relevant for low-latency and DPDK-style workloads.

Practical advice to close with: set memory request == memory limit (memory doesn't compress, so bursting on it just means being killed later at a worse time), set a CPU request from observed p90-ish usage, review with actual data from `kubectl top` / VPA recommendations rather than guessing, and remember that over-requesting is the most common source of cloud waste while under-requesting is the most common source of noisy-neighbour incidents. Newer Kubernetes versions support in-place pod resizing for CPU/memory without recreating the pod, which is gradually removing the "resize means restart" tradeoff.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sizing-example }
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: api:1.8.3
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "500m"          # scheduling reservation + cgroup weight under contention
          memory: "1Gi"
        limits:
          # cpu intentionally omitted for a latency-sensitive service (avoid CFS throttling)
          memory: "1Gi"        # == request: memory does not compress, so don't pretend it does
      env:
        - name: GOMEMLIMIT
          value: "900MiB"      # tell the runtime the ceiling; don't let it discover it via OOM
# QoS here = Burstable (cpu limit missing). Set cpu limit 500m too and it becomes Guaranteed.

---
# What the kernel actually enforces (cgroup v2, on the node)
# /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/.../cpu.max     -> "50000 100000"  = 500m
# /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/.../cpu.weight  -> derived from the request
# /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/.../memory.max  -> 1073741824

# ---- Diagnosing kills and throttling ----
kubectl get pod api-xxxx -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pod api-xxxx -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}{"\n"}'
# {"exitCode":137,"reason":"OOMKilled","startedAt":...,"finishedAt":...}
kubectl describe pod api-xxxx | grep -E 'Last State|Reason|Exit Code|Restart Count'

kubectl top pods -n payments --sort-by=memory      # requires metrics-server
kubectl top nodes

# Throttling is invisible without metrics -- these are the PromQL queries to know:
#   rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m])
#     / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m])           > 0.25  => throttled hard
#   container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.9  => OOM soon

# Right-sizing input: what did it actually use over a week?
#   quantile_over_time(0.95, rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{pod=~"api-.*"}[5m])[7d:5m])
#   max_over_time(container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~"api-.*"}[7d])

sections.title: 18. Probes: Liveness, Readiness, Startup — and How to Get Them Wrong
sections.content:
Three probes, three completely different consequences, and confusing them is one of the most common causes of self-inflicted outages.

**Readiness** answers "should this pod receive traffic right now?" On failure, kubelet marks the container not-ready, the EndpointSlice controller removes the pod IP from the Service's endpoints, and traffic stops arriving. The pod is **not** restarted. This is the traffic gate — it is what makes rolling updates safe (new pods only count as Available once ready) and what lets a pod temporarily shed load (warming a cache, a full request queue, waiting on a dependency at startup).

**Liveness** answers "is this container wedged beyond recovery?" On failure, kubelet **kills and restarts the container**, in place, on the same node. It is a deadlock detector, nothing more. The default answer to "what should my liveness probe check?" is: as little as possible — usually a trivial endpoint that proves the event loop or request thread is still turning. It should never touch a database, another service, or anything else outside the process. The reason is the failure mode: if your liveness probe checks the database and the database has a bad five minutes, **every pod of every service that depends on it fails liveness and restarts simultaneously**, turning a degraded dependency into a total, cluster-wide outage that then hammers the recovering database with reconnect storms. A dependency being down is a *readiness* condition at most, and often not even that.

**Startup** answers "has this container finished booting?" While a startup probe is configured and not yet succeeding, liveness and readiness probes are suspended. It exists to solve a specific problem: a JVM or a service loading a large model may take three minutes to start, but once running should be declared dead after ten seconds of unresponsiveness. Without a startup probe you'd have to set `initialDelaySeconds: 180` on the liveness probe, which means for the first three minutes of *every* restart, a genuinely hung process is not detected. With a startup probe you set a generous `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` budget for boot (e.g. 30 × 10s = 5 minutes) and keep the liveness probe tight afterwards.

Handlers: `httpGet` (any 200–399 is success; you can set headers and use a named port), `tcpSocket` (connection established = success — weak, since a hung server still accepts connections), `exec` (exit 0 = success; note this forks a process in the container on every period, which is genuinely expensive at high frequency and is a known source of CPU noise), and `grpc` (native support for the standard gRPC health checking protocol, so you no longer need to ship `grpc_health_probe`).

Timing fields and their defaults: `initialDelaySeconds: 0`, `periodSeconds: 10`, `timeoutSeconds: 1`, `successThreshold: 1` (must be 1 for liveness and startup), `failureThreshold: 3`. Do the arithmetic — worst-case detection time is roughly `initialDelay + failureThreshold × period`, and the timeout is per attempt. The default `timeoutSeconds: 1` is aggressively short for anything that does real work under load; a probe that occasionally takes 1.2 s will restart your container at the worst possible moment, i.e. when it is already overloaded. That is the second classic self-inflicted outage: **liveness probes that fail under load, restarting pods that were merely busy, removing capacity, and increasing load on the survivors** — a textbook cascading failure. Guard against it with a generous timeout, a `failureThreshold` of 3+, and a liveness endpoint that does no I/O.

Two more real-world notes. Probes are executed by kubelet from the node, not from another pod — so they bypass Services and NetworkPolicy between pods, but they are affected by whether the container is listening on the right interface (bind `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1`). And a pod that is `1/1 Running` but getting no traffic is almost always a readiness probe that never passed: check `kubectl get pod -o wide` READY column, then the endpoints.
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: probes-done-right }
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: registry.example.com/api:1.8.3
      ports: [{ name: http, containerPort: 8080 }]

      # Boot budget: 30 * 10s = up to 5 minutes to start. Liveness/readiness are
      # suspended until this passes, so slow starts never trigger a restart loop.
      startupProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http }
        periodSeconds: 10
        failureThreshold: 30

      # DEADLOCK DETECTOR ONLY. No DB. No downstream calls. Generous timeout.
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http }   # returns 200 if the server loop is alive
        periodSeconds: 10
        timeoutSeconds: 5                          # default of 1s is too tight under load
        failureThreshold: 3                        # ~30s to declare death

      # TRAFFIC GATE. May check local warm-up state and (carefully) critical deps.
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: http }
        periodSeconds: 5
        timeoutSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 2                        # drop out of endpoints fast
        successThreshold: 1

---
# gRPC services: native probe, no grpc_health_probe binary needed
      livenessProbe:
        grpc: { port: 9000, service: "" }          # standard grpc.health.v1.Health
        periodSeconds: 10

---
# ANTI-PATTERN -- do not ship this:
      livenessProbe:
        exec:
          command: ["sh","-c","curl -sf http://db:5432 && curl -sf http://auth/healthz"]
      # A 5-minute DB blip now restarts every pod of every dependent service at once.

# Triage
kubectl get pods -o wide                       # READY 0/1 with STATUS Running => readiness failing
kubectl describe pod api-xxxx | grep -A3 -E 'Liveness|Readiness|Startup'
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Unhealthy --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
#   Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
#   Normal   Killing    Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted

sections.title: 19. Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (and the Rest of the Autoscaling Story)
sections.content:
The HorizontalPodAutoscaler is a controller that periodically (about every 15 seconds) reads a metric, computes a desired replica count, and writes it to the target's `scale` subresource. Because it drives the standard `scale` subresource it works on Deployments, StatefulSets, ReplicaSets and any CRD that exposes one — it does not work on DaemonSets, which have exactly one pod per node by definition.

The algorithm is one line and you should be able to state it: `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue)`. If 10 pods average 90% CPU and the target is 60%, you get `ceil(10 × 90/60) = 15`. A **tolerance** (10% by default) suppresses scaling when the ratio is within that band, so the HPA doesn't churn on noise. Only pods that are Ready and have metrics count; pods still starting up are excluded so they don't drag the average down and cause runaway scale-up.

For `type: Resource` with `averageUtilization`, utilization is measured **as a percentage of the pod's CPU request**, not of the node or of the limit. Two consequences interviewers love: if a container has no CPU request, utilization is undefined and the HPA reports `unknown` and refuses to scale; and if your requests are wildly off, your target percentage means something different than you think — halve every request and every pod suddenly reads as 200% utilised. Resource metrics come from **metrics-server** via `metrics.k8s.io` (an aggregated API); if metrics-server isn't installed, `kubectl top` fails and so does the HPA. Custom and external metrics (`custom.metrics.k8s.io`, `external.metrics.k8s.io`) come from an adapter like the Prometheus Adapter or KEDA, and are usually the *right* signal: queue depth, requests per second per pod, or p99 latency correlate with user pain far better than CPU does. KEDA additionally handles scale-to-zero and event-source-driven scaling (Kafka lag, SQS depth, cron), which plain HPA does not do by default.

Stability is controlled by the `behavior` block. Scale-up has no stabilization window by default (react fast), while scale-down uses a **300-second stabilization window** — the controller takes the *maximum* desired replica count computed over the last 5 minutes, so it only shrinks when demand has genuinely stayed low. You can tighten or loosen both, and add rate policies (`Pods: 4 per 60s`, `Percent: 100 per 60s`) with `selectPolicy: Max|Min|Disabled`. Aggressive scale-down is a classic incident generator: traffic dips for 90 seconds, you shed 60% of capacity, traffic returns, and now you're cold-starting under load.

Failure modes worth naming. **HPA versus GitOps**: if your Deployment manifest pins `replicas: 3` and Argo CD or a `kubectl apply` re-asserts it, the HPA and your CD system will fight forever. Omit `replicas` from the managed manifest (or configure the CD tool to ignore that field). **HPA versus VPA** on the same resource metric is explicitly unsupported — the VPA raises requests, which lowers measured utilization, which makes the HPA scale in, which raises per-pod load, which makes the VPA raise requests. Use VPA for memory and HPA for CPU/custom metrics, or use neither together on the same axis. **HPA cannot help if there is nowhere to put the pods**: it will happily set replicas to 40 and leave 25 of them Pending. That is the **Cluster Autoscaler**'s job (or Karpenter's) — it watches for unschedulable pods and adds nodes, and removes nodes that have been underutilised for a while and whose pods can move. The two autoscalers are complementary and both need honest requests to work, because Cluster Autoscaler simulates scheduling using requests. Finally, remember that horizontal scaling only helps if the bottleneck is per-pod. Adding pods in front of a saturated single-writer database makes the outage worse, and that is exactly the kind of judgement an interviewer is probing for.
sections.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: api, namespace: payments }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api                       # the Deployment manifest must NOT pin spec.replicas
  minReplicas: 4                    # floor for redundancy, not just for load
  maxReplicas: 60                   # guard against a metric bug bankrupting you
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 }   # % of the CPU *request*
    - type: Pods                    # custom per-pod metric via prometheus-adapter
      pods:
        metric: { name: http_requests_per_second }
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "250" }
    - type: External                # e.g. Kafka consumer lag from an external source
      external:
        metric:
          name: kafka_consumergroup_lag
          selector: { matchLabels: { topic: payments, group: settle } }
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "1000" }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }   # can double every 30s
        - { type: Pods,    value: 8,   periodSeconds: 30 }
      selectPolicy: Max
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600      # be slow and boring on the way down
      policies:
        - { type: Percent, value: 10, periodSeconds: 60 }

# When the HPA does nothing, read its status -- it says exactly why:
kubectl describe hpa api -n payments
#   Metrics: resource cpu on pods (as a percentage of request): <unknown> / 60%
#   ScalingActive  False  FailedGetResourceMetric: missing request for cpu
#   ScalingLimited True   TooManyReplicas: the desired count is above maxReplicas

kubectl get hpa -A
kubectl top pods -n payments                       # proves metrics-server works
kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes | head -c 400
kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics             # must be Available=True

sections.title: 20. StatefulSets: Stable Identity, Ordered Rollouts, and Per-Pod Storage
sections.content:
A Deployment treats its pods as interchangeable: random name suffixes, no ordering, all sharing whatever volumes are declared, replaced freely. That model is wrong for clustered stateful systems, where a specific replica owns a specific data directory and other members need to address it by a name that survives restarts. A StatefulSet provides four guarantees that a Deployment does not.

**Stable identity.** Pods are named `<sts>-0` … `<sts>-(N-1)` and keep that name across reschedules. Combined with a **headless Service** (which the StatefulSet must name in `spec.serviceName`), each pod gets a stable DNS record `<sts>-<ordinal>.<service>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`. Note it is the *name* that is stable, not the IP — the pod IP changes when it moves, which is exactly why DNS matters here. Systems like ZooKeeper, Kafka, etcd, Cassandra, and most primary/replica databases are configured with a fixed member list, and this is what makes that possible.

**Stable per-pod storage.** `volumeClaimTemplates` makes the controller create one PVC per pod, deterministically named `<template>-<sts>-<ordinal>` (e.g. `data-mysql-0`). When `mysql-0` is rescheduled to another node, it re-binds to *the same* PVC and therefore the same data. Critically, **scaling down does not delete the PVCs** — that is a deliberate safety choice, so scaling 5→3 and back to 5 reattaches the original volumes rather than starting empty. It also means shrinking a StatefulSet silently leaves you paying for orphaned disks; newer versions add `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` so you can opt into deletion on scale-down or on StatefulSet deletion.

**Ordered, sequential operations.** With the default `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady`, pod N is created only after pod N-1 is Running and Ready, and scale-down proceeds in reverse (highest ordinal first). Rolling updates likewise proceed from the highest ordinal downwards, waiting for each pod to be Ready before touching the next. The consequence to name in an interview: **one pod that never becomes Ready blocks the entire rollout**, permanently, and a stuck StatefulSet rollout usually means a broken readiness probe or a pod that can't mount its volume — not a controller bug. Set `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` when your system doesn't need bootstrap ordering (it affects creation/deletion, not update ordering).

**Controlled updates.** `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: N` updates only pods with ordinal >= N. Set `partition` to `replicas-1` to update exactly one pod as a canary, verify it, then lower the partition to roll the rest. `OnDelete` disables automatic updates entirely — the new template applies only when you delete a pod yourself, which is what many database operators prefer.

The important caveats. A StatefulSet gives identity and storage; it does **not** give you replication, leader election, backups, or failover. Those are the database's job, which is why the industry uses **operators** (CloudNativePG, Strimzi, Vitess, etc.) — a StatefulSet plus a controller that understands the system's semantics. Also, node failure handling is deliberately conservative: when a node goes unreachable, `mysql-0`'s pod is marked `Terminating` but is *not* recreated, because Kubernetes cannot distinguish "node is dead" from "node is partitioned but still writing to the disk," and recreating the pod elsewhere would risk two writers on one dataset (split-brain). You must fence the node — apply the `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taint, or otherwise confirm death — before the pod is recreated. Finally, `RWO` volumes attach to exactly one node, so a StatefulSet pod is pinned to wherever its disk can attach; in a multi-zone cluster this means the pod is effectively zone-pinned, which is why `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` matters so much.
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: mysql }
spec:
  clusterIP: None                # headless -> per-pod DNS, required by the StatefulSet
  selector: { app: mysql }
  ports: [{ name: mysql, port: 3306 }]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: mysql }
spec:
  serviceName: mysql             # must match the headless Service name
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady        # or Parallel if no bootstrap ordering is needed
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 0               # set to 2 to canary only mysql-2, then lower to 0
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenScaled: Retain           # Delete would remove PVCs when you scale in
    whenDeleted: Retain
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: mysql } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: mysql } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120     # give the DB time to flush and shut down
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: mysql } }
      containers:
        - name: mysql
          image: mysql:8.4
          ports: [{ name: mysql, containerPort: 3306 }]
          volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/mysql }]
          readinessProbe:
            exec: { command: ["mysqladmin","ping","-h","127.0.0.1"] }
            periodSeconds: 5
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3
        resources: { requests: { storage: 200Gi } }

# Identity you can rely on:
#   pods : mysql-0, mysql-1, mysql-2
#   PVCs : data-mysql-0, data-mysql-1, data-mysql-2
#   DNS  : mysql-0.mysql.prod.svc.cluster.local

kubectl get sts mysql -o jsonpath='{.status.currentRevision} {.status.updateRevision}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pvc -l app=mysql            # survive scale-down on purpose
kubectl rollout status sts/mysql
kubectl patch sts mysql --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}'   # canary the top ordinal

sections.title: 21. DaemonSets: One Pod per Node, Including Nodes That Don't Exist Yet
sections.content:
A DaemonSet ensures that every node matching a selector runs exactly one copy of a pod. Add a node to the cluster and the DaemonSet controller immediately creates a pod for it; remove the node and the pod goes with it. That "including future nodes" property is the whole point, and it is why cluster infrastructure is packaged this way: CNI agents (Calico, Cilium), kube-proxy itself, log collectors (Fluent Bit, Vector), metrics agents (node-exporter, Datadog), CSI node plugins, and security agents.

Two implementation details are worth knowing because they explain otherwise confusing behaviour. First, since v1.12 DaemonSet pods are scheduled by the **default scheduler**, not placed directly by the DaemonSet controller: the controller creates the pod with a `nodeAffinity` term pinning it to one specific node, and the scheduler does the rest. This means DaemonSet pods respect priority, preemption and resource fit like anything else — a node with no room left will leave the DaemonSet pod Pending, which is why infrastructure DaemonSets should carry `priorityClassName: system-node-critical` so they can preempt application pods rather than being starved by them.

Second, the DaemonSet controller **automatically adds a set of tolerations** to its pods so that agents keep running on nodes that are in trouble: `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready` and `unreachable` (NoExecute, no timeout, so they aren't evicted from a failing node), plus `disk-pressure`, `memory-pressure`, `pid-pressure`, and `unschedulable` (NoSchedule). That is deliberate — you specifically want your log shipper alive on a node that's melting down. It also means DaemonSet pods are *not* removed by `kubectl drain`, which is why the command requires `--ignore-daemonsets`. What the controller does **not** add is a toleration for control-plane taints or your custom taints; to run an agent on control-plane or GPU-tainted nodes you must add those tolerations yourself.

Targeting a subset of nodes is done with `spec.template.spec.nodeSelector` or node affinity — for example, only nodes labelled `hardware=gpu` get the NVIDIA device plugin. Updates use `updateStrategy: RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable` (default 1), meaning the rollout walks node by node; on a 500-node cluster with a slow-starting agent that can take hours, so `maxUnavailable: 10%` (and optionally `maxSurge`) is a normal tuning. `OnDelete` is the manual alternative for agents where you want to control timing per node.

Design notes people get wrong. A DaemonSet is the right shape only when the workload is genuinely per-node — reading `/var/log/containers` from a hostPath, listening on the node's network, or programming the node's kernel. If you use a DaemonSet merely to "have a copy everywhere" for a stateless HTTP service, you have coupled your replica count to your node count and given up autoscaling. Also, DaemonSet pods commonly need elevated access (hostPath mounts, `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, capabilities like `NET_ADMIN`), which makes them the highest-value target in the cluster: a compromised node agent with `hostPath: /` is a full node takeover. Keep their images tiny, their RBAC minimal, and their Pod Security exemptions explicit rather than cluster-wide. Finally, size their requests carefully — a DaemonSet's resource request is multiplied by every node in the cluster, so an extra 200 MiB of memory request across 500 nodes is 100 GiB of capacity you can no longer schedule application pods into.
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit
  namespace: logging
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: fluent-bit } }
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 10%            # default is 1 -- far too slow on a large cluster
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: fluent-bit } }
    spec:
      priorityClassName: system-node-critical   # must not be preempted off a busy node
      serviceAccountName: fluent-bit
      # Automatic tolerations cover not-ready / unreachable / *-pressure / unschedulable.
      # You must add anything else yourself:
      tolerations:
        - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
        - key: nvidia.com/gpu
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/os: linux
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 96Mi }   # x every node in the cluster -- be honest
            limits:   { memory: 192Mi }
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: varlog,     mountPath: /var/log,                 readOnly: true }
            - { name: containers, mountPath: /var/lib/docker/containers, readOnly: true }
          securityContext:
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath: { path: /var/log }             # the reason this is a DaemonSet at all
        - name: containers
          hostPath: { path: /var/lib/docker/containers }

# Operating
kubectl -n logging get ds fluent-bit
# DESIRED CURRENT READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE NODE SELECTOR
#   42      42      41      42        41     kubernetes.io/os=linux
kubectl -n logging get pods -l app=fluent-bit -o wide --field-selector status.phase!=Running
kubectl get nodes -l kubernetes.io/os=linux --no-headers | wc -l   # should equal DESIRED
kubectl drain node7 --ignore-daemonsets        # required: drain will not evict DS pods

sections.title: 22. Jobs and CronJobs: Run-to-Completion Work
sections.content:
A Job runs pods until a specified number of them **succeed**, then stops. That is a fundamentally different contract from a Deployment, which is a steady-state controller and will restart your batch process forever. `restartPolicy` in a Job's pod template must be `OnFailure` or `Never` — `Always` is rejected, because "always restart" and "run to completion" are contradictory.

The parallelism model is two fields. `completions` is how many successful pod completions are needed; `parallelism` is how many pods may run at once. `completions: 1` is a one-shot task. `completions: 100, parallelism: 10` is a work queue processed ten at a time. Omitting `completions` while setting `parallelism` gives the "worker pool" pattern: pods run until *any* one of them exits successfully, which suits a queue where workers exit when the queue drains. `completionMode: Indexed` gives each pod a fixed index from 0 to completions-1, exposed as the annotation/env `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` and in the pod's hostname — that's how you statically shard work (pod 3 processes partition 3) without any external coordinator.

Failure handling has more nuance than people expect. `backoffLimit` (default 6) is the number of *pod* failures tolerated before the whole Job is marked Failed; retries back off exponentially (10s, 20s, 40s, … capped at six minutes), so hitting the default limit takes a surprisingly long time. Note the interaction with `restartPolicy: OnFailure`: the container restarts in place on the same node and pod, so a crash-looping container can burn a lot of wall-clock time before it counts as a pod failure. `restartPolicy: Never` creates a fresh pod per attempt, which leaves the failed pods around for inspection — usually what you want for debugging. `activeDeadlineSeconds` puts a hard wall-clock cap on the Job regardless of retries (and takes precedence over `backoffLimit`). Newer versions add `podFailurePolicy`, which lets you distinguish "the container exited 42, that's a permanent config error, fail immediately without wasting six retries" from "the pod was preempted/evicted by the infrastructure, don't count that against the backoff limit" — extremely valuable on spot instances. `backoffLimitPerIndex` does the same per-index for Indexed Jobs.

Cleanup matters operationally: finished Jobs and their pods are **not** deleted automatically unless you set `ttlSecondsAfterFinished`. Thousands of Completed pods from a per-minute CronJob is a real, common source of etcd bloat and slow `kubectl get pods`.

A **CronJob** is a thin controller that creates Jobs on a schedule (standard 5-field cron syntax, with a `timeZone` field so you don't have to reason in UTC). Its important fields: `concurrencyPolicy` — `Allow` (default; overlapping runs are permitted, which is the right answer for "my hourly job now takes 70 minutes and there are three of them running"), `Forbid` (skip the new run if the previous is still active), or `Replace` (kill the old, start the new); `startingDeadlineSeconds`, which bounds how late a missed run may still be started; and `successfulJobsHistoryLimit` (3) / `failedJobsHistoryLimit` (1) for retention. `suspend: true` pauses scheduling, which is how you disable a job during an incident without deleting it.

The guarantee to be honest about in an interview: **a CronJob is not exactly-once.** The controller can miss a window (control plane down, `startingDeadlineSeconds` exceeded — and if more than 100 schedules are missed it gives up and logs an error rather than stampeding), and it can in principle create two Jobs for one schedule. Idempotency has to live in your job: use a lock, a unique run key, or an upsert, and never assume a nightly billing job runs precisely once. Two more traps: a CronJob's schedule is evaluated by the controller, so a Job that starts is guaranteed only to have been *created* on time, not to have been *scheduled* onto a node on time; and, before native sidecar containers, any injected sidecar (service mesh proxy, log agent) would keep running after the main container exited, leaving the pod alive forever and the Job never completing — the fix on modern clusters is native sidecars, and on older ones an explicit shutdown call to the sidecar's admin endpoint from the main container's exit path.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: { name: reindex }
spec:
  completions: 100
  parallelism: 10
  completionMode: Indexed        # each pod gets JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX 0..99
  backoffLimit: 6
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600    # hard wall-clock cap for the whole Job
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600   # auto-clean 10 min after finishing
  podFailurePolicy:
    rules:
      - action: FailJob          # exit 42 = permanent config error: stop immediately
        onExitCodes: { containerName: worker, operator: In, values: [42] }
      - action: Ignore           # spot reclaim: don't count against backoffLimit
        onPodConditions:
          - { type: DisruptionTarget }
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never       # fresh pod per attempt; failures stay around to inspect
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: registry.example.com/reindex:2.3
          command: ["/app/reindex", "--shard=$(JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX)", "--shards=100"]
          env:
            - name: JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.annotations['batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index'] }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }

---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: { name: nightly-billing }
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  timeZone: "Europe/London"          # otherwise the controller's clock (UTC) decides
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid          # never two billing runs at once
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 900       # if we couldn't start within 15 min, skip this window
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  suspend: false                     # flip to true to pause during an incident
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: bill
              image: registry.example.com/billing:4.1
              # NOTE: args are NOT shell-expanded by Kubernetes -- "$(...)" is env-var
              # substitution, not a shell. Use an explicit shell if you need date math.
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
              args:
                - /app/bill --date="$(date -d yesterday +%F)"
                          --idempotency-key="nightly-$(date -d yesterday +%F)"

# Operating
kubectl create job --from=cronjob/nightly-billing billing-manual-2026-01-05   # run it now
kubectl patch cronjob nightly-billing -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'
kubectl get jobs --sort-by=.status.startTime
kubectl describe job reindex | grep -E 'Pods Statuses|Completions'
kubectl logs job/reindex --all-containers --tail=50
kubectl get pods -l job-name=reindex --field-selector=status.phase=Failed

sections.title: 23. RBAC and Workload Identity
sections.content:
Kubernetes authorization for the API is role-based and made of exactly four object kinds, which is why the model is easy to state and easy to get subtly wrong.

A **Role** is a namespaced list of permissions: `apiGroups` × `resources` (optionally `resourceNames`) × `verbs` (`get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`, `deletecollection`, plus special ones like `impersonate`, `escalate`, `bind`, and subresource verbs). A **ClusterRole** is the same thing without a namespace, and it serves three purposes: granting access to cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces), granting access across all namespaces, and being a reusable permission *template*. A **RoleBinding** grants a Role — **or a ClusterRole** — to subjects *within one namespace*; binding a ClusterRole via a RoleBinding is the single most useful idiom in RBAC, because you define `edit`-like permissions once and grant them per namespace. A **ClusterRoleBinding** grants a ClusterRole cluster-wide. There is no "deny" rule: RBAC is purely additive, and the union of all your bindings is your access.

Rules are **not** hierarchical or wildcard-magical in the way people assume. `verbs: ["get"]` does not imply `list`, and code that calls `kubectl get pods` (a LIST) will be denied by a role granting only `get`. Subresources are separate strings: `pods/log`, `pods/exec`, `pods/portforward`, `deployments/scale`. Granting `pods/exec` is effectively granting a shell inside any container in that namespace, which is a much bigger deal than it looks in a YAML diff.

Identity comes in two flavours. **ServiceAccounts** are real, namespaced Kubernetes objects and are how *workloads* authenticate; every pod gets one (`default` if unspecified) and the token is projected into the pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/`. Modern clusters use **bound tokens**: short-lived, audience-scoped JWTs issued by the TokenRequest API and refreshed by kubelet, rather than the old permanent Secret-based tokens (auto-created SA token Secrets were removed as a default in v1.24). **Human users** are *not* Kubernetes objects at all — they are just a username and groups extracted from a client certificate or an OIDC token, which is why you can't `kubectl delete user` and why cert-based access is hard to revoke without a CRL or a CA rotation. `system:masters` is a group that bypasses authorization entirely.

RBAC has built-in **privilege-escalation prevention**, which surprises people: you cannot create or edit a Role granting permissions you do not already hold, unless you have the `escalate` verb on roles; and you cannot create a binding to a role whose permissions exceed yours unless you have `bind`. Otherwise anyone with "manage RBAC in my namespace" would be cluster-admin in one step.

The escalation paths a security-minded interviewer wants you to name: `get secrets` in a namespace means reading every credential there, including ServiceAccount tokens if any legacy ones exist; `create pods` in a namespace means you can mount **any** ServiceAccount in that namespace and inherit its permissions — plus mount `hostPath: /` and read the node's kubelet credentials if Pod Security doesn't stop you; `pods/exec` bypasses everything by putting you inside a running container; `create/update` on `validatingwebhookconfigurations` or `mutatingwebhookconfigurations` lets you intercept and rewrite every API request in the cluster; and `escalate`/`bind`/`impersonate` are self-explanatory. The mitigations are least-privilege roles per workload, Pod Security admission at `restricted`, a NodeRestriction-enabled Node authorizer so kubelets can only read what concerns their own node, and audit logging.

For cloud API access, don't put static cloud keys in Secrets. Map the pod's ServiceAccount to a cloud identity — IRSA on EKS, Workload Identity on GKE/AKS — so the pod exchanges its projected, expiring Kubernetes token for short-lived cloud credentials. That converts a stolen Secret into a stolen 15-minute token.

# Namespaced read-only role for an app's ServiceAccount
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: config-reader, namespace: payments }
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]          # NOTE: get does NOT imply list
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    resourceNames: ["db-credentials"]        # narrow to one object
    verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/payments-api   # IRSA
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { name: api-config-reader, namespace: payments }
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: config-reader
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: api
    namespace: payments
---
# The key idiom: define once as a ClusterRole, grant per-namespace with a RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { name: devs-edit, namespace: payments }
roleRef: { apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, kind: ClusterRole, name: edit }
subjects:
  - { kind: Group, name: "payments-devs", apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }
---
# Pods should not get an API token unless they call the API
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: api
  automountServiceAccountToken: false        # default true -- turn it off for most workloads

# ---- Auditing ----
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:payments:api -n payments
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=jane@example.com -n payments
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin")
  | "\(.metadata.name): \(.subjects // [] | map(.kind+"/"+.name) | join(", "))"'
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o wide | grep -i 'cluster-admin\|system:masters'

# Escalation check: who can read secrets or exec anywhere?
kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] | select(.rules[]? | (.resources[]? | test("secrets|pods/exec")))
  | .metadata.name'

sections.title: 24. Placement Control: Taints, Tolerations, Affinity, Spread, and PDBs
sections.content:
Kubernetes gives you two directions of control over placement, and interviewers like this topic because it's easy to state the difference and easy to blur it.

**Taints and tolerations are node-side repulsion.** A taint on a node says "keep pods off unless they explicitly opt in." Effects: `NoSchedule` (no new pods without a matching toleration), `PreferNoSchedule` (soft), and `NoExecute` (also *evicts* already-running pods that don't tolerate it — with `tolerationSeconds` giving a grace period). A toleration on a pod is only permission; it does **not** attract the pod to that node. This is the number-one confusion: tainting your GPU nodes stops normal workloads landing there, but a GPU pod with only a toleration may still be scheduled onto a cheap CPU node. To *require* placement you need node affinity (or a resource request only those nodes satisfy, like `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`). Kubernetes also uses taints internally: `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready`, `unreachable`, `memory-pressure`, `disk-pressure`, `unschedulable` (set by `kubectl cordon`), and cloud providers' `node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized`.

**Affinity is pod-side attraction.** `nodeSelector` is the primitive version (exact label match, hard). **Node affinity** is the expressive version, with `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` (hard filter, supports `In`, `NotIn`, `Exists`, `Gt`, `Lt`) and `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` (weighted soft preference). Note the `IgnoredDuringExecution` half of every one of those names: these rules are evaluated **only at scheduling time**, so relabelling a node never moves a running pod. **Pod affinity/anti-affinity** places pods relative to other pods using a `topologyKey` — "schedule me in the same zone as pods labelled `app=cache`" (affinity) or "never put two of my replicas on the same node" (anti-affinity with `topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname`). Be aware that inter-pod affinity is computationally expensive: the scheduler must evaluate pods across matching topology domains for every candidate node, and on large clusters heavy use measurably slows scheduling.

For spreading, prefer **`topologySpreadConstraints`** over anti-affinity. Anti-affinity is binary — "at most one per domain" — so with 3 zones and 10 replicas, required anti-affinity leaves 7 pods Pending forever. Spread constraints express degree: `maxSkew: 1` over `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` means the busiest zone may hold at most one more pod than the emptiest, which is exactly the intent. `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` makes it a hard constraint; `ScheduleAnyway` makes it a scoring preference (place as evenly as possible but never block). Real production configs typically use `DoNotSchedule` with `maxSkew: 1` across zones and `ScheduleAnyway` across hostnames. Watch out for a subtle failure: with `DoNotSchedule` across zones, if one zone's nodes are full or the zone is down, new pods can become unschedulable rather than piling into the healthy zones — that's the tradeoff you're choosing.

**PriorityClass** decides who wins when there isn't room: higher `value` schedules first, and by default may **preempt** (evict) lower-priority pods to fit. `preemptionPolicy: Never` gives queue priority without eviction rights. Reserve high values for genuinely critical paths; hand them out widely and you get eviction churn.

**PodDisruptionBudgets** are the other half of availability and are frequently forgotten. A PDB declares how much of a workload may be voluntarily disrupted at once (`minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable`), and the **Eviction API** — used by `kubectl drain`, cluster autoscaler scale-down, and node upgrade tooling — refuses to evict a pod if doing so would violate it. PDBs do not protect against a kernel panic, a spot reclaim (which may not go through eviction), or your own `kubectl delete pod`; they cover *voluntary* disruption only. Two operational gotchas: a PDB with `minAvailable` equal to the replica count blocks all drains forever (a very common cause of "the node upgrade has been stuck for six hours"), and a PDB matching a workload whose pods are already unhealthy also blocks drains, because evicting one would push availability below the floor.
sections.code:
# --- Node side: taint a GPU pool so ordinary work stays away ---
kubectl taint nodes gpu-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule
kubectl label  nodes gpu-1 hardware=gpu topology.kubernetes.io/zone=eu-west-1a

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: trainer, labels: { app: trainer } }
spec:
  # 1) Permission to land on tainted nodes (does NOT attract)
  tolerations:
    - { key: gpu, operator: Equal, value: "true", effect: NoSchedule }

  affinity:
    # 2) Requirement to land on GPU nodes (this is what actually attracts)
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - { key: hardware, operator: In, values: ["gpu"] }
      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - weight: 50
          preference:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, operator: In, values: ["p4d.24xlarge"] }

    # 3) Keep replicas off the same node
    podAntiAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: trainer } }
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

  # 4) Even spread across zones -- expresses DEGREE, unlike anti-affinity
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: trainer } }
    - maxSkew: 2
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway        # soft: never block on this one

  priorityClassName: latency-critical
  containers:
    - name: train
      image: trainer:3.0
      resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 } }

---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: trainer }
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1          # NOT minAvailable == replicas, or drains block forever
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: trainer } }

# Why is this drain stuck?
kubectl get pdb -A
# NAME     MIN AVAILABLE  ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS
# trainer  N/A            0                     <- 0 means nothing can be evicted
kubectl describe pdb trainer
kubectl taint nodes gpu-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule-      # trailing '-' removes a taint

sections.title: 25. Storage: Volumes, PV, PVC, StorageClass, and CSI
sections.content:
Container filesystems are ephemeral: the writable layer dies with the container, and `emptyDir` dies with the pod. Anything that must outlive a pod needs a **PersistentVolume**.

The model separates three concerns. A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is a cluster-scoped object representing a real piece of storage (an EBS volume, a Ceph RBD image, an NFS export). A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a namespaced request for storage — "I want 100 GiB, ReadWriteOnce, from class `gp3`" — and it is what a pod references. A **StorageClass** describes a *kind* of storage, naming the provisioner and its parameters, and enables **dynamic provisioning**: instead of an admin pre-creating PVs, the external provisioner watches for unbound PVCs referencing its class, creates the real volume in the backend, and creates the matching PV. Binding is exclusive and one-to-one: once a PVC binds to a PV, no other claim can use it, and a PVC bound to a 100 GiB PV when it asked for 50 GiB simply gets the whole thing.

**Access modes** describe how many *nodes* can mount the volume, not how many pods: `ReadWriteOnce` (one node — multiple pods on that same node can share it), `ReadOnlyMany`, `ReadWriteMany` (many nodes, which most block storage cannot do; you need NFS, CephFS, EFS, Azure Files), and `ReadWriteOncePod` (exactly one pod, useful when a second writer would corrupt data). Getting this wrong produces the classic `Multi-Attach error for volume ... volume is already exclusively attached to one node` when a Deployment with an RWO PVC does a rolling update: the new pod lands on a different node and cannot attach until the old pod fully terminates. That's why RWO + `Deployment` + `RollingUpdate` is a trap — use `Recreate`, or a StatefulSet, or RWX storage.

**`volumeBindingMode`** is the field that separates people who've run multi-zone clusters from those who haven't. With the default `Immediate`, the volume is provisioned as soon as the PVC is created — possibly in zone A — and then the pod might be schedulable only in zone B, where that disk cannot attach, leaving the pod Pending forever. **`WaitForFirstConsumer`** delays provisioning until a pod using the claim is scheduled, so the provisioner creates the disk in the right zone, honouring the pod's affinity and resource constraints. Nearly every modern cloud StorageClass should use it.

**`reclaimPolicy`** governs what happens to the PV when its PVC is deleted: `Delete` (destroy the underlying volume — the default for most dynamic classes, and a fine way to lose a database) or `Retain` (keep the PV and data, marked `Released`, requiring manual cleanup before reuse). Production databases should use `Retain` or, better, be protected by backups plus `Retain`. `allowVolumeExpansion: true` permits growing a PVC by editing `spec.resources.requests.storage`; most CSI drivers now support online expansion (the filesystem grows without a pod restart). You cannot shrink.

Everything real is implemented through **CSI**, the out-of-tree plugin interface: a *controller* component (Deployment/StatefulSet) that creates, deletes, attaches and snapshots volumes, plus a *node* component (DaemonSet) that stages and mounts them on each node, wrapped by standard Kubernetes sidecars (`external-provisioner`, `external-attacher`, `external-resizer`, `external-snapshotter`). This is why storage failures usually appear as events on the pod — `FailedAttachVolume`, `FailedMount`, `Unable to attach or mount volumes: timed out waiting for the condition` — and the diagnosis moves to the CSI controller logs and the cloud API.

Finally, know the ephemeral options and their sharp edges. `emptyDir` lives on the node's disk (or in RAM with `medium: Memory`, where it counts against the pod's memory limit) and is deleted with the pod; always set `sizeLimit`, because an unbounded `emptyDir` filling a node's disk triggers `DiskPressure` and evicts everything on that node. `hostPath` mounts a node path directly and is a serious security hole in general workloads (mount `/var/run/docker.sock` or `/` and you own the node) — legitimate only for node agents. And the `pvc-protection` finalizer means a PVC still referenced by a running pod will sit in `Terminating` rather than being deleted, which is a feature, not a bug.
