apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3
  annotations: { storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" }
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "6000"
  throughput: "250"
  encrypted: "true"
reclaimPolicy: Delete             # use Retain for anything you would cry about losing
allowVolumeExpansion: true
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer   # provision in the zone the pod actually lands in
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: pgdata, namespace: payments }
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]  # ONE NODE, not one pod
  storageClassName: gp3
  resources: { requests: { storage: 200Gi } }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: legacy-app }
spec:
  strategy: { type: Recreate }    # RWO + RollingUpdate => Multi-Attach errors on every deploy
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: legacy } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: legacy } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { fsGroup: 2000 }        # chown the mount so a non-root app can write
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: legacy:1.0
          volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/app }]
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: pgdata }

# ---- Operating ----
kubectl get pvc,pv -n payments
kubectl get pvc pgdata -o jsonpath='{.status.phase} {.spec.volumeName}{"\n"}'   # Pending? see events
kubectl describe pvc pgdata          # "waiting for first consumer" is NORMAL with WaitForFirstConsumer
kubectl describe pod legacy-xxxx | grep -A5 Events
#   Warning FailedAttachVolume  Multi-Attach error for volume "pvc-9c1..."
#   Warning FailedMount         Unable to attach or mount volumes: timed out waiting for the condition

# Online expansion (grow only -- never shrink)
kubectl patch pvc pgdata -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"400Gi"}}}}'
kubectl get pvc pgdata -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[*].type}{"\n"}'   # FileSystemResizePending

# Rescue a Released PV whose PVC was deleted (reclaimPolicy: Retain)
kubectl patch pv pvc-9c1... -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'    # makes it Available again

# CSI plumbing
kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l app=ebs-csi-controller -c csi-provisioner --tail=50

sections.title: 26. The Pod Network Model and NetworkPolicy
sections.content:
Kubernetes deliberately specifies networking as a set of *requirements*, not an implementation, and every conforming CNI plugin must satisfy them: every pod gets its own IP address; pods can communicate with all other pods on any node **without NAT**; agents on a node (kubelet, node agents) can reach all pods on that node; and the IP a pod sees itself as is the IP others see it as. This "flat IP space" is why there's no port mapping in Kubernetes the way there is in plain Docker — two pods can both listen on port 8080 because they're in different network namespaces with different IPs.

Implementations vary widely under that contract. Overlay networks (VXLAN/Geneve, as in Flannel or Calico's overlay mode) encapsulate pod traffic inside node-to-node packets, which works anywhere but costs a little throughput and reduces the effective MTU — a classic source of "small requests work, large POSTs hang" bugs when MTU is misconfigured. Native routing modes (Calico with BGP, or cloud CNIs like AWS VPC CNI and Azure CNI) give pods real VPC IPs with no encapsulation, which is faster and makes pods directly addressable from outside the cluster, at the cost of consuming VPC address space (and, on EKS, a per-instance-type limit on pod density driven by ENI/IP allocation). eBPF-based CNIs (Cilium) implement forwarding, policy and even service load balancing in kernel BPF programs, and can replace kube-proxy entirely.

**NetworkPolicy** is the namespaced object that restricts pod-to-pod traffic, and its semantics are the part interviewers test. The default is *allow all*. A NetworkPolicy selects pods with `podSelector`, and the moment **any** policy selects a pod for a given direction, that pod becomes **default-deny for that direction**, and only traffic explicitly permitted by some policy is allowed. Policies are purely additive — there are no deny rules and no ordering or priority — so the effective permission set is the union of all policies selecting the pod. An empty `podSelector: {}` selects every pod in the namespace, which is how you write the standard default-deny baseline. Also note `policyTypes`: a policy with only `ingress` rules doesn't restrict egress at all unless you list `Egress` in `policyTypes`.

Peers come in three forms and one of them causes constant bugs: `podSelector` (pods in the *same* namespace as the policy), `namespaceSelector` (all pods in matching namespaces), and `ipBlock` (CIDR, with `except`). Writing `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` as two items in a list means OR; nesting them under a single list item means AND ("pods labelled `app=api` **in** namespaces labelled `env=prod`"). The YAML difference is one dash, and getting it wrong silently opens a policy far wider than intended.

Practical guidance for production. Adopt default-deny per namespace, then add explicit allows — but remember the two things that break immediately: **DNS egress** (if you deny egress and forget to allow UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS in `kube-system`, every name resolution in the namespace fails, and the symptom looks like a total application outage) and **health/monitoring scrapes** (kubelet probes come from the node, which is usually fine, but Prometheus scraping from another namespace must be allowed explicitly). Also know the limits: NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 only — no HTTP paths, no methods, no identity beyond IP/labels; it is enforced by the CNI, so on a plugin that doesn't implement it your policies are silently inert (a genuinely dangerous failure mode worth testing for); egress rules to external services by DNS name aren't in the core API, so you either use CIDRs, a plugin-specific FQDN policy, or an egress gateway. For L7 rules, mTLS between services, and identity-based policy, that's the service mesh's job — and the newer cluster-scoped `AdminNetworkPolicy` API exists to let platform teams set baseline rules that namespace owners can't override.
sections.code:
# 1) Baseline: default-deny BOTH directions for every pod in the namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny-all, namespace: payments }
spec:
  podSelector: {}                 # every pod in this namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]  # no rules listed => nothing allowed
---
# 2) The one everybody forgets: DNS must be allowed or the namespace goes dark
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-dns-egress, namespace: payments }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
          podSelector:        { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
# 3) Allow the ingress controller in, and the api pods out to the DB only
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: api-policy, namespace: payments }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        # AND: pods labelled app=ingress-nginx INSIDE namespaces labelled name=ingress
        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { name: ingress } }
          podSelector:       { matchLabels: { app: ingress-nginx } }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } }   # same namespace
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except: ["10.0.0.0/8", "169.254.169.254/32"]     # block RFC1918 + cloud metadata
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]

# CAREFUL -- this is OR, not AND (a leading dash on each selector):
#   from:
#     - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { name: ingress } }
#     - podSelector:       { matchLabels: { app: ingress-nginx } }
#   => "any pod in namespace 'ingress'" OR "any pod labelled app=ingress-nginx anywhere in THIS ns"

# Verify policies actually do something (they are inert on CNIs that ignore them)
kubectl run probe --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -n payments -- \
  sh -c 'nc -zv postgres 5432; nc -zv -w2 example.com 80; nslookup api'
kubectl get networkpolicies -n payments
kubectl describe networkpolicy api-policy -n payments

sections.title: 27. Debugging Playbook: Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, and Friends
sections.content:
Almost every pod problem announces itself in `STATUS`, and each status has a small, well-defined set of causes. The discipline is: read the status, read `kubectl describe` events, read logs (including `--previous`), and only then start guessing.

**Pending** means the pod exists in the API but has not been bound to a node, or has been bound but the sandbox hasn't started. If `spec.nodeName` is empty, the scheduler couldn't place it, and `kubectl describe pod` gives you the exact tally: `0/9 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {...}, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector`. Work the categories: **insufficient resources** (requests too large, cluster genuinely full, or a request bigger than any single node's allocatable — the last one never resolves, no matter how long you wait or how many nodes you add); **taints** (need a toleration, or the nodes are cordoned); **affinity/selector** mismatch (typo in a node label is the usual cause); **unbound PVC** (`pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims` — but note that with `WaitForFirstConsumer` a PVC that says "waiting for first consumer" is normal and not the problem); **hostPort conflicts**; and **topology spread** with `DoNotSchedule` unable to be satisfied. If the pod *is* scheduled but stuck at `ContainerCreating`, the problem is on the node: image pull, volume attach/mount, CNI failing to allocate an IP (`failed to allocate for range 0: no IP addresses available in range` means the node's pod CIDR is exhausted), or a missing ConfigMap/Secret.

**ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull** is exactly what it says, and the describe output includes the registry's actual error. The causes: a typo'd image name or tag; a private registry with no `imagePullSecret` on the pod or its ServiceAccount (`pull access denied` / `authentication required`); Docker Hub anonymous rate limits (`toomanyrequests`); a manifest that has no variant for the node's CPU architecture (build multi-arch or pin the right one; the alternate symptom is `exec format error` at start); a registry unreachable because of a NetworkPolicy, proxy, or private-endpoint issue; and `imagePullPolicy: Always` on a node that has lost registry access even though the image is already cached locally. Remember the default policy: `IfNotPresent`, except when the tag is `:latest` or omitted, where it becomes `Always`.

**CrashLoopBackOff** is not an error in itself — it means the container has exited repeatedly and kubelet is now waiting before the next restart, backing off 10s, 20s, 40s … up to a 5-minute cap (reset after the container stays up long enough). The information you need is the previous container's exit code and logs: `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`. Then map the exit code: **137** = SIGKILL, almost always the memory limit (check `lastState.terminated.reason: OOMKilled`) or a SIGKILL after a grace-period timeout; **143** = SIGTERM, a clean-ish external stop; **1** or **2** = application error, read the logs; **126** = the command exists but isn't executable; **127** = command not found (wrong path, wrong base image, a binary built for glibc running on Alpine's musl); **0** with a restart loop = the process finished successfully but `restartPolicy: Always` restarts it anyway — you wrote a batch job as a Deployment. Also check the obvious environment causes: a missing env var, a config file that isn't mounted where the app expects, a permission error because `runAsNonRoot` conflicts with a volume's ownership (`fsGroup` fixes that), or a port already in use on `hostNetwork`.

Then there is the pod that looks fine and isn't. `1/1 Running` but no traffic is a readiness problem or an endpoint/selector problem — check `kubectl get endpointslices`. `0/1 Running` for a long time is a readiness probe that never passes. `Init:0/2` is an init container failing, so read *its* logs with `-c`. `Terminating` forever is a finalizer, a wedged container that ignores SIGTERM, or a dead node. `Evicted` is node pressure — usually disk, not memory. `CreateContainerConfigError` is a missing ConfigMap/Secret key. `Completed` with restarts is a Job-shaped workload in a Deployment.

The two modern debugging tools worth naming: **ephemeral containers** (`kubectl debug -it pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app`) attach a debug container that shares the target's namespaces, which is the only way to get a shell into a distroless or read-only container that has no shell of its own; and `kubectl debug node/<node>` gives you a privileged pod in the node's namespaces with its filesystem at `/host` — the right way to inspect a node without SSH.
sections.code:
# ============ THE FIRST FOUR COMMANDS, ALWAYS ============
kubectl get pods -o wide                                  # STATUS, READY, RESTARTS, NODE
kubectl describe pod <pod>                                # events at the bottom = the answer
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>                         # current process
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous              # THE CRASHED ONE -- most people forget

kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30 # cluster-wide, last hour only

# ============ PENDING ============
kubectl describe pod <pod> | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
#  0/9 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint, 2 didn't match affinity
kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/Events/p'   # requests, not usage
kubectl get pvc                                            # Pending PVC blocks the pod
kubectl get nodes --show-labels | tr ',' '\n' | grep -i <your-label>

# ============ IMAGEPULLBACKOFF ============
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 Failed
#  Failed to pull image "reg/api:1.8.3": ... unauthorized: authentication required
kubectl get sa default -o jsonpath='{.imagePullSecrets}{"\n"}'
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password="$TOKEN"
kubectl patch sa default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
crictl pull registry.example.com/api:1.8.3    # test the pull from the node itself

# ============ CRASHLOOPBACKOFF ============
kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=100
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}{"\n"}'
# {"exitCode":137,"reason":"OOMKilled",...}      -> raise memory limit / fix the leak
# exit 127 command not found | 126 not executable | 1 app error | 0 + Always = wrong workload type

# Run the image with a different entrypoint to inspect it without the app crashing:
kubectl debug <pod> -it --copy-to=<pod>-debug --container=app -- sh
kubectl run shell --rm -it --image=<same-image> --restart=Never --command -- sh

# ============ NO SHELL IN THE IMAGE (distroless / readOnlyRootFilesystem) ============
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app -- bash
#   shares the target container's network + process namespaces

# ============ NODE-LEVEL ============
kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox     # privileged pod, node fs at /host
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A8 Conditions
journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager           # (on the node)

# ============ SERVICE NOT REACHABLE ============
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>   # empty => labels or readiness
kubectl get pods -l <svc-selector> -o wide --show-labels
kubectl run probe --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c 'nslookup <svc>; curl -sv http://<svc>:80/healthz'
kubectl get networkpolicies -A

# ============ STUCK TERMINATING ============
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}{"\n"}'
kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=0 --force     # LAST RESORT: only when the node is dead;
                                                      # for StatefulSets this risks two writers.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through exactly what happens when you run `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`.
interviewQA.a:
kubectl reads your kubeconfig, discovers the API resource from the API server's discovery endpoints, computes a patch (three-way merge against the `last-applied-configuration` annotation, or a server-side apply with field ownership), and sends an HTTPS request.

The API server runs a fixed pipeline: authenticate the caller (client cert, bearer token, OIDC), authorize the verb/resource/namespace via RBAC, run mutating admission (built-ins like ServiceAccount token injection and LimitRanger defaults, plus any mutating webhooks such as a mesh sidecar injector), validate against the schema, run validating admission (ResourceQuota, Pod Security, validating webhooks / CEL policies), and then persist the object to etcd. That write is the only durable state change; nothing else has happened yet.

From there everything is watch-driven. The Deployment controller sees the new object, hashes the pod template, and creates a ReplicaSet named `<deploy>-<hash>` with `pod-template-hash` injected into its selector and pod labels. The ReplicaSet controller sees 3 desired / 0 existing and creates 3 Pod objects with `ownerReferences` pointing back at it; those pods have no `nodeName`. The scheduler watches for unbound pods, filters out nodes that can't run them (resources based on requests, taints, affinity, volume topology, ports), scores the survivors, and writes a Binding that sets `spec.nodeName`.

The kubelet on that node sees a pod assigned to itself: it pulls images, asks the container runtime over CRI to create a pod sandbox (the pause container), which invokes CNI to allocate an IP and wire up the network namespace, mounts volumes, runs init containers to completion, then starts the app containers, and continuously writes container status back into the pod's `status`. Once readiness probes pass, the EndpointSlice controller adds the pod IP to matching Services' EndpointSlices, and kube-proxy on every node updates its dataplane rules so the ClusterIP starts routing there.

The key architectural point: no component ever calls another component. Everything coordinates by reading and writing objects through the API server, and every loop is level-triggered, so any of them can crash and resume without special recovery logic.
followUps: Which of those steps still work if the API server is down?
Where exactly would a mutating webhook fit, and what happens if that webhook is unavailable?
How does the Deployment controller avoid the new and old ReplicaSets stealing each other's pods?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and what goes wrong if you configure them badly?
interviewQA.a:
Readiness answers "should this pod receive traffic?" — failing it removes the pod from the Service's EndpointSlices but does not restart anything. Liveness answers "is this container wedged?" — failing it makes kubelet kill and restart the container in place. Startup is a third probe that suspends the other two until the app has finished booting, so you can allow a five-minute start while still detecting a hang within thirty seconds afterwards.

The most damaging misconfiguration is a liveness probe that checks external dependencies. If `/healthz` queries the database and the database has a bad five minutes, every pod of every dependent service fails liveness simultaneously and restarts, so a degraded dependency becomes a total outage — and the restart storm then hammers the recovering database with reconnection attempts. A liveness probe should be as close to "is my event loop turning" as possible: no downstream calls, no I/O.

The second common failure is liveness probes that trip under load. The default `timeoutSeconds` is 1 second, which is far too tight for a busy service; a probe that occasionally takes 1.2s will restart a container that was merely busy, removing capacity and increasing load on the survivors — textbook cascading failure. Use a generous timeout, `failureThreshold` of 3 or more, and a handler that does no real work.

The third is having no readiness probe at all. Without one, pods are considered Ready the moment their containers start, so a rolling update will replace all your healthy old pods with new ones that are still booting, and `maxUnavailable` becomes meaningless. Readiness is what makes rolling updates safe, and pairing it with `minReadySeconds` is what stops a pod that is ready-then-immediately-crashing from being counted as Available.

Finally, a readiness probe can legitimately fail on a dependency (shedding traffic while unable to serve), but even that should be considered carefully — if every replica de-registers at once you have no capacity at all and no error page either.
followUps: What are the defaults for periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds and failureThreshold, and how long does it take to detect a hang with them?
Why would you add a startup probe instead of just raising initialDelaySeconds on the liveness probe?
A pod shows 1/1 Running but gets no traffic. Where do you look?
How do probes interact with a pod that is terminating?

interviewQA.q: A pod is stuck in Pending. How do you debug it?
interviewQA.a:
First establish whether it is unscheduled or scheduled-but-not-started: check `spec.nodeName`. If it's empty, the scheduler couldn't place it, and `kubectl describe pod` gives you a precise per-node tally in the FailedScheduling event, something like `0/9 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {gpu: true}, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector`. That single line accounts for every node and tells you which category to chase.

The categories are: **insufficient resources** — the pod's requests don't fit in any node's remaining allocatable; note the scheduler works from *requests*, not usage, so a node can be 5% utilised and still full. If the request exceeds any single node's allocatable, the pod will never schedule no matter how many nodes you add. **Taints** — need a matching toleration, or the nodes are cordoned (`node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable`). **Affinity/nodeSelector mismatch** — usually a typo'd or missing node label; verify with `kubectl get nodes --show-labels`. **Volume topology** — `pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims`, or the PV exists in a different zone than the pod can run in. **hostPort conflicts.** **Topology spread** with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` that can't be satisfied. And **ResourceQuota** rejections, which don't show on the Deployment at all — you have to look at the ReplicaSet's events for `exceeded quota`.

If the pod *is* bound to a node but stuck in `ContainerCreating`, the problem is node-side: image pull failure, volume attach/mount timeout, CNI unable to allocate an IP (node pod-CIDR exhaustion), or a referenced ConfigMap/Secret that doesn't exist (`CreateContainerConfigError`).

If capacity genuinely is the problem, the fix is either right-sizing requests or adding nodes — and that's the Cluster Autoscaler's or Karpenter's job, not the HPA's. The HPA will happily set replicas to 40 and leave 25 of them Pending.
followUps: How would you tell the difference between "the cluster is full" and "this pod can never fit on any node"?
What does `WaitForFirstConsumer` do, and why does a PVC that says "waiting for first consumer" not indicate a problem?
A Deployment says 3 desired but only 1 pod exists and there is no event on the Deployment. Where is the error?

interviewQA.q: Explain CrashLoopBackOff. How do you actually diagnose it?
interviewQA.a:
CrashLoopBackOff isn't an error condition of its own — it's kubelet saying "this container keeps exiting, so I'm waiting before restarting it again." The backoff doubles from 10s to 20s to 40s and so on, capped at five minutes, and resets once the container stays up. The interesting information is always about the *previous* run.

So: `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` for the crashed container's output, and `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}'` for the exit code and reason. Then map the exit code. **137** is SIGKILL, and with `reason: OOMKilled` it's the memory cgroup limit — either the limit is too low or you have a leak; note that the runtime's own heap sizing matters here, since a JVM or Node process that sizes itself against the node's RAM rather than the container limit gets killed reliably. 137 without OOMKilled usually means the container ignored SIGTERM and was killed at the end of the grace period. **143** is SIGTERM. **1** or **2** is a plain application error — read the logs. **126** means the entrypoint isn't executable, **127** means command not found, which is very often a binary compiled against glibc running on an Alpine/musl base, or a wrong path in the Dockerfile. **Exit 0 with restarts** means the process completed successfully but `restartPolicy: Always` restarts it — you've deployed a batch job as a Deployment.

Then check the environment causes that produce identical symptoms: a missing env var or config file (frequently a `subPath` mount pointing at the wrong key), a permission failure because the container runs as non-root but the volume is owned by root (`fsGroup` fixes it), a port collision on `hostNetwork`, or a dependency the app refuses to start without.

If the image has no shell — distroless, or a read-only root filesystem — use `kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app`, which attaches an ephemeral container sharing the target's namespaces. To inspect the image itself without the app crashing, run it with an overridden command, or `kubectl debug --copy-to=<pod>-debug` and change the entrypoint.

One important distinction: a failing *liveness probe* also produces repeated restarts, but the events say `Killing container ... failed liveness probe` rather than the app exiting on its own. That's a probe problem, not an application crash.
followUps: What exit code do you see for an OOM kill, and how do you confirm it was the cgroup limit rather than the node running out of memory?
How do you get a shell into a distroless container?
How would you distinguish a crash loop from a liveness-probe restart loop?
The container exits 0 immediately. What have you probably done wrong?

interviewQA.q: Explain requests versus limits, and the QoS classes that come out of them. Should you set CPU limits?
interviewQA.a:
A request is a scheduling reservation — the scheduler sums the requests of pods assigned to a node and refuses to place a pod whose requests don't fit in `allocatable`. A limit is a runtime cap enforced by the kernel through cgroups. They're enforced by different subsystems at different times, and the two resources behave completely differently.

CPU is compressible. The request becomes a cgroup weight (`cpu.shares` / `cpu.weight`), which only matters under contention — an unlimited container on an idle node can use the whole machine. The limit becomes CFS bandwidth: N microseconds of CPU per 100ms period. Blow through the quota and *every thread in the container is frozen until the next period*. That's throttling: a latency event, not an error, invisible unless you're watching `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total`. Multi-threaded runtimes suffer badly — 8 threads against a 1-core limit exhaust the period's budget in 12.5ms and then stall for 87.5ms.

Memory is incompressible. The request is scheduling-only; the limit becomes `memory.max`, and exceeding it means the kernel OOM-kills the process immediately, exit 137, no chance to handle it.

QoS classes derive from that. **Guaranteed**: every container sets both requests and limits for both CPU and memory, and they're equal. **Burstable**: some requests set, but not Guaranteed. **BestEffort**: nothing set at all. QoS drives the OOM score adjustment (so under node-level memory exhaustion the kernel eats BestEffort first) and kubelet's node-pressure eviction order (BestEffort, then Burstable pods over their requests, then Guaranteed). Guaranteed pods with integer CPU limits also get exclusive cores under the static CPU manager policy.

On CPU limits, the defensible position is: always set CPU requests; be deliberate about CPU limits. For latency-sensitive services on a cluster where requests are set honestly, the request-based weighting already provides fair sharing under contention, and adding a limit mostly buys you throttling at the worst possible moment. Set CPU limits where predictability or hard tenant isolation outranks tail latency, or where you're protecting against a runaway. For memory, set request equal to limit — memory doesn't compress, so "bursting" on it just means being killed later at a worse time.
followUps: What exactly is CFS throttling, and how would you detect it in Prometheus?
Which QoS class does a pod get if one of two containers sets resources and the other doesn't?
If a node runs out of memory, in what order do pods die, and what's the difference between eviction and an OOM kill?
How do you pick a memory limit for a JVM or Node.js service?

interviewQA.q: How does a rolling update work, and how do you guarantee zero downtime during a deploy?
interviewQA.a:
The Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet for the new pod template and shifts replicas between the two, bounded by `maxSurge` (how far above `replicas` total pods may go, default 25%) and `maxUnavailable` (how far below `replicas` *available* pods may drop, default 25%). Each step: scale the new RS up within the surge budget, wait for the new pods to become Available, scale the old RS down within the unavailable budget, repeat.

Zero downtime needs four things, and the interviewer is listening for all of them.

First, a **readiness probe**. Without one, a pod counts as Ready the instant it starts, so the controller cheerfully replaces healthy old pods with new ones that are still booting. `minReadySeconds` on top of that stops a pod that is ready-then-immediately-failing from counting as Available.

Second, **`maxUnavailable: 0`** (with a nonzero `maxSurge`) if you can afford the extra capacity — this guarantees you never dip below your full replica count.

Third, **graceful shutdown, including a `preStop` sleep**. When a pod is deleted, endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen *in parallel*, and endpoint removal has to propagate to kube-proxy on every node and to every ingress controller and mesh sidecar. So the pod can start shutting down while traffic is still being routed to it, producing connection refused errors during every deploy. A `preStop` hook that sleeps 5–15 seconds keeps the pod serving while endpoints converge, and only then does SIGTERM arrive. Your app must then drain: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, exit — and it must actually *receive* SIGTERM, which means being PID 1 or behind a proper init, not behind a shell that swallows signals.

Fourth, **PodDisruptionBudgets and spread**, so that node drains and cluster autoscaler scale-downs during the deploy can't take out the rest of your capacity.

For long-lived connections (gRPC, WebSockets, HTTP keep-alive) none of the above is sufficient, because clients hold an open TCP connection straight to the pod IP. The server has to send GOAWAY or `Connection: close` and let clients reconnect through the Service.

Finally: rollouts don't auto-rollback. A broken image stalls the rollout at `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` with most old pods still serving; a release that passes readiness but returns 500s rolls all the way out. That's why real canary tooling watches error-rate SLIs and aborts automatically.
followUps: What exactly is the race between endpoint removal and SIGTERM, and why does a preStop sleep fix it?
What happens if the new pods never become Ready — does Kubernetes roll back automatically?
How would you do a canary rather than a plain rolling update?
Why doesn't a rolling update help clients holding long-lived gRPC connections?

interviewQA.q: What actually happens when a pod is deleted? Walk me through the termination sequence.
interviewQA.a:
The API server sets `metadata.deletionTimestamp` and the grace period clock starts; the pod's phase display becomes `Terminating`. Then two things happen **concurrently**, with no ordering between them.

On one side, the pod is marked not-ready and the EndpointSlice controller removes its address from every Service that selected it. That change then has to propagate — to kube-proxy on every node, to ingress controllers that watch endpoints directly, to mesh sidecars with their own endpoint tables. That propagation is not instant and not bounded by anything Kubernetes promises.

On the other side, kubelet runs the `preStop` hook (if any) and then sends SIGTERM to PID 1 of each container. When `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` expires — the default is 30, and the preStop hook's runtime is *inside* that budget — kubelet sends SIGKILL. Once the runtime confirms the containers are gone, kubelet reports back, the API server removes the object, and only then does the pod actually disappear.

The consequences worth stating. **The race**: because endpoint removal isn't sequenced before SIGTERM, requests can still be routed to a pod that has begun shutting down. The standard fix is a `preStop` hook that just sleeps a few seconds, keeping the container fully functional while endpoints converge. **PID 1 semantics**: if the container's entrypoint is a shell, the shell is PID 1 and typically doesn't forward SIGTERM, so nothing happens for 30 seconds and then everything is SIGKILLed mid-request. Use exec-form CMD or a small init like tini. **Native sidecars** are shut down after the main containers, which is one of the reasons they were introduced — previously the mesh proxy could exit first and break the app's outbound draining.

Two edge cases: a pod whose node is unreachable stays `Terminating` indefinitely, because deletion isn't finalised until a kubelet confirms the containers are gone and there is no kubelet — for a StatefulSet that's deliberate, since recreating the pod could give you two writers on one disk. And a pod with finalizers stays until every finalizer is removed by its owning controller. Force-deleting with `--grace-period=0 --force` skips confirmation entirely and should be treated as a last resort with real data-corruption risk for stateful workloads.
followUps: Does the preStop hook run before or after SIGTERM, and is it inside or outside the grace period?
Why does a pod on a dead node stay Terminating, and how do you resolve it safely?
What happens if your process ignores SIGTERM entirely?

interviewQA.q: Explain ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, headless Services, and Ingress. When do you use each?
interviewQA.a:
They stack. **ClusterIP** is the base: a virtual IP from the service CIDR, reachable only inside the cluster. Nothing listens on it — it's purely DNAT rules programmed into every node's packet path by kube-proxy, which is why you usually can't ping it and never see it on the wire. **NodePort** is a ClusterIP plus a port in the 30000–32767 range opened on every node, forwarding to the Service; it's mostly a building block, or a bare-metal escape hatch. **LoadBalancer** is a NodePort plus a cloud load balancer provisioned by the cloud-controller-manager; one per Service, which is why running fifty of them is expensive. **ExternalName** is different in kind — no proxying, just a CNAME returned by CoreDNS, useful for pointing a cluster-internal name at an external hostname. **Headless** (`clusterIP: None`) means no VIP and no kube-proxy involvement; DNS returns the ready pod IPs directly, which is what StatefulSets need for stable per-pod names and what clients that do their own load balancing (gRPC, database drivers) want.

**Ingress** sits above all of this: one HTTP(S) entry point routing by host and path to many Services, with central TLS termination — so you pay for one cloud load balancer instead of fifty. It's inert without an ingress controller installed, which is the most common gotcha; the object just sits there with a blank ADDRESS.

Selection logic in practice: ClusterIP for anything internal; headless when the client wants the individual endpoints; LoadBalancer for a single non-HTTP TCP/UDP service that must be exposed externally; Ingress (or Gateway API) for HTTP, which is nearly everything user-facing. Reach for Gateway API on new clusters, because Ingress's core spec covers so little that everything real ends up in controller-specific annotations, and Gateway API makes header matching, weighted splits and mirroring typed fields with a clean split between platform-owned Gateways and team-owned Routes.

One more thing to say because it separates candidates: a Service load-balances **per TCP connection**, not per request. An HTTP/2 or gRPC client that opens a single long-lived connection pins to one pod indefinitely, no matter how many replicas you run. The fixes are headless plus client-side load balancing, an L7 proxy or mesh, or periodic connection recycling.
followUps: What does `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` change, and what does it cost you?
Why does a Service not balance gRPC traffic evenly?
What's the difference between kube-proxy's iptables and IPVS modes?
Where do Ingress controllers actually send traffic — the ClusterIP or the pod IPs?

interviewQA.q: I've created a Service but nothing can reach it. How do you debug that?
interviewQA.a:
Work outward from the backend, because the failure is almost always in the first two checks.

**One: does the Service have endpoints?** `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>` (or the Endpoints summary in `kubectl describe svc`). Empty endpoints means the Service isn't finding backends, and there are exactly three causes: the Service's `selector` doesn't match the pod labels (remember it selects *pod* labels, not the Deployment name, and there's no referential integrity so a typo fails silently); the pods exist but aren't Ready, because the readiness probe never passes; or the pods are in a different namespace, since a Service only selects within its own.

**Two: is the port mapping right?** `port` is what clients dial, `targetPort` is the container port. A mismatch gives you endpoints that exist but connections that are refused. `targetPort` can be a named port, which is more robust.

**Three: does DNS resolve?** Test from inside a pod in the caller's namespace: `nslookup <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`. If short names fail but FQDNs work, look at `dnsPolicy` — host-network pods need `ClusterFirstWithHostNet` or they use the node's resolver and can't see cluster DNS at all.

**Four: connectivity.** `curl` the ClusterIP and then a pod IP directly from a debug pod (`kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot`). If the pod IP works and the ClusterIP doesn't, suspect kube-proxy on that node. If neither works, the app may be bound to `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0` inside the container.

**Five: NetworkPolicy.** Once any policy selects a pod for a direction, that direction becomes default-deny. Check policies in both namespaces, and specifically check that DNS egress to CoreDNS is allowed — a missing DNS egress rule looks exactly like a total outage.

**Six, for external access**: is it a LoadBalancer with a pending EXTERNAL-IP (no cloud controller, or quota exhausted)? Is it an Ingress with a blank ADDRESS (no ingress controller installed, or the wrong `ingressClassName`)? With `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, are there pods on the nodes the LB is health-checking?
followUps: The endpoints list is empty but the pods are Running. What are the two most likely causes?
How would you prove the problem is DNS rather than connectivity?
What's the fastest way to test a ClusterIP from outside the cluster?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret, and how do updates propagate to running pods?
interviewQA.a:
Structurally they're nearly the same object; Secrets store values base64-encoded and get somewhat better handling — mounted from tmpfs, redacted in some tooling, separately encryptable at rest — but **base64 is encoding, not encryption**. Anyone who can `get` the Secret, or read etcd, reads the value.

Propagation depends entirely on how you project it. **As environment variables**, values are read once at container start and baked into the process environment; they never update, full stop. Change the ConfigMap and the running pod keeps the old value forever. Env vars also leak readily — `/proc/<pid>/environ`, crash dumps, child processes. **As a volume**, kubelet does keep the files updated, atomically, by writing a new timestamped directory and swapping the `..data` symlink; the delay is up to the kubelet sync period (about a minute by default) plus cache time. The critical exception is that **`subPath` mounts never receive updates**, because they bypass the symlink indirection — that's why mounting a single config file with `subPath` and expecting live reloads doesn't work.

And even with volume updates, the application has to notice the file changed and reload it, which most don't.

So the pattern that actually works in production is to treat config as immutable and roll pods on change: name the ConfigMap with a content hash, reference that name from the Deployment, and a config change becomes a normal, versioned, observable, rollback-able rolling update. Helm's `checksum/config` annotation and Kustomize's `configMapGenerator` hash suffix do exactly this. Marking the object `immutable: true` is complementary: it forbids edits and lets kubelet stop watching it, which is a real API-server load reduction at scale.

For Secrets specifically, the things worth saying: turn on encryption at rest with a KMS provider; treat `get secrets` in a namespace as equivalent to "read every credential in that namespace" when writing RBAC; note that `create pods` in a namespace is nearly as powerful, since you can mount any ServiceAccount there; prefer short-lived credentials — projected ServiceAccount tokens with an audience and expiry, IRSA/Workload Identity for cloud APIs, Vault or the Secrets Store CSI driver for dynamic database credentials — over long-lived static values; and never commit plaintext secrets to Git (use SOPS/Sealed Secrets, or the External Secrets Operator syncing from a real secret manager).
followUps: Why doesn't a `subPath` mount get updates?
What does `immutable: true` buy you?
Are Secrets encrypted at rest by default? How would you change that?
How would you rotate a database password with zero downtime?

interviewQA.q: When do you need a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?
interviewQA.a:
When individual replicas are not interchangeable — when replica N owns a specific dataset and other members need to address it by a name that survives rescheduling. A StatefulSet gives you four things a Deployment doesn't:

**Stable identity**: pods are `sts-0` … `sts-(N-1)` and keep those names forever; combined with the required headless Service, each gets a stable DNS record `sts-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local`. Note that the *name* is stable, not the IP — which is precisely why DNS matters for clustered systems configured with a fixed member list.

**Stable per-pod storage**: `volumeClaimTemplates` produce one PVC per pod, deterministically named, so when `mysql-0` is rescheduled it rebinds to *its* data. Scaling down deliberately does not delete PVCs, so 5→3→5 reattaches the original volumes rather than starting empty (which also means orphaned disks you keep paying for, unless you set `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy`).

**Ordered operations**: with `OrderedReady`, pod N starts only after N-1 is Ready, scale-down goes highest-ordinal-first, and rolling updates walk downwards waiting for readiness at each step. The corollary an interviewer wants: one pod that never becomes Ready blocks the entire rollout, permanently.

**Controlled updates** via `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition`, which lets you canary the highest ordinal and then lower the partition, or `OnDelete` for fully manual control.

Two things to be honest about. A StatefulSet provides identity and storage — it does **not** provide replication, leader election, failover, or backups. Those are the database's semantics, which is why real deployments use operators (CloudNativePG, Strimzi, Vitess) that combine a StatefulSet with a controller that understands the system. And node-failure handling is deliberately conservative: when a node goes unreachable, the pod is marked Terminating and is *not* recreated, because Kubernetes can't distinguish a dead node from a partitioned one that's still writing to disk. You have to fence the node — the `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taint — before the pod comes back elsewhere.

Conversely, don't use a StatefulSet just because your app writes some files. If replicas are interchangeable and share nothing, a Deployment with a PVC (or object storage) is simpler and rolls out faster.
followUps: Why does scaling a StatefulSet down not delete the PVCs?
What is the headless Service for, and what breaks without it?
A node dies and `mysql-0` is stuck Terminating. Why won't Kubernetes just recreate it?
How do you canary a single replica of a StatefulSet?

interviewQA.q: How does the HorizontalPodAutoscaler decide how many replicas to run, and where does it go wrong?
interviewQA.a:
Every 15 seconds or so it reads the metric and computes `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric)`, with a 10% tolerance band to suppress churn. Only Ready pods with metrics count. It then writes the result to the target's `scale` subresource — which is why it works on Deployments, StatefulSets and any CRD with a scale subresource, but not on DaemonSets.

For CPU utilization targets, the crucial detail is that utilization is a percentage **of the pod's CPU request**, not of the node or the limit. So a container with no CPU request produces `<unknown>` and the HPA refuses to scale, and halving all your requests makes every pod read as twice as utilised. Resource metrics come from metrics-server via the aggregated `metrics.k8s.io` API; if that's missing or unhealthy, both `kubectl top` and the HPA stop working.

Stability comes from the `behavior` block: scale-up has no stabilization window by default, while scale-down uses a 300-second window, taking the maximum desired value over that period so it only shrinks when demand has genuinely stayed low. You can add rate policies (`Percent`/`Pods` per period) in both directions. Over-eager scale-down is a real incident generator: shed 60% of capacity during a 90-second dip and you cold-start under returning load.

The failure modes to name: **fighting with GitOps**, if your Deployment manifest pins `replicas` and Argo CD keeps re-asserting it — omit the field or configure the tool to ignore it. **HPA plus VPA on the same metric** is explicitly unsupported and forms a feedback loop, since VPA raising requests lowers measured utilization. **No capacity** — the HPA will set replicas to 40 and leave 25 Pending; adding nodes is the Cluster Autoscaler's or Karpenter's job. **Wrong signal** — CPU often doesn't correlate with user pain; queue depth, RPS per pod, or concurrency usually do, which means custom metrics via the Prometheus Adapter or KEDA. **`minReplicas` too low** for redundancy, or `maxReplicas` unbounded so a metrics bug scales you into a very large bill.

And the judgement point: horizontal scaling helps only when the bottleneck is per-pod. Adding replicas in front of a saturated single-writer database makes the outage worse, not better.
followUps: What happens if a container has no CPU request and you target CPU utilization?
Why is the scale-down stabilization window 300 seconds by default?
What breaks if both an HPA and a VPA target the same Deployment?
How do you autoscale on queue depth instead of CPU?

interviewQA.q: Explain RBAC: Role vs ClusterRole, RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding. How do you debug a `forbidden` error?
interviewQA.a:
A Role is a namespaced set of permissions — `apiGroups` × `resources` × `verbs`, optionally narrowed with `resourceNames`. A ClusterRole is the same without a namespace, and it serves three purposes: access to cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces), access across all namespaces, and being a reusable permission template. A RoleBinding grants a Role *or a ClusterRole* to subjects within one namespace; a ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole cluster-wide. Binding a ClusterRole through a RoleBinding is the key idiom — define the permission set once, grant it per namespace.

Three properties people get wrong. RBAC is purely additive with **no deny rules**, so your effective access is the union of every binding. Verbs are **not** hierarchical: `get` does not imply `list`, and a controller doing a LIST will be denied by a role that only grants `get`. And subresources are separate resource strings — `pods/log`, `pods/exec`, `pods/portforward`, `deployments/scale` — so granting `pods/exec` is effectively granting a shell in every container in that namespace.

Identity: ServiceAccounts are real namespaced objects and are how workloads authenticate, with short-lived audience-bound projected tokens on modern clusters. Human users are *not* objects at all — just a username and groups derived from a client cert or OIDC token, which is why you can't delete a user and why cert-based access is hard to revoke. The `system:masters` group bypasses authorization entirely.

To debug a `forbidden`, read the message — it states the user, the verb, the resource, and the namespace, and that's usually enough. Then reproduce with impersonation: `kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>`, and `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=...` to see everything that identity has. Common causes: the pod is using the `default` ServiceAccount because `serviceAccountName` was omitted; a RoleBinding in the wrong namespace; a ClusterRole that covers the resource but was bound with a RoleBinding so it only applies in one namespace; the resource is cluster-scoped so a Role can never grant it; a missing `list`/`watch` verb; or the wrong `apiGroup` (Deployments are in `apps`, not `""`).

Worth adding: RBAC has built-in escalation prevention — you can't create a role granting permissions you don't hold unless you have the `escalate` verb, and you can't bind such a role without `bind`.
followUps: Why can a RoleBinding reference a ClusterRole, and what's the effect?
Name three RBAC permissions that are effectively cluster-admin in disguise.
How do you find out which ServiceAccount a running pod is using and what it can do?
How do you revoke access for a human user who authenticates with a client certificate?

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between taints/tolerations, node affinity, and topology spread constraints?
interviewQA.a:
They solve different halves of the placement problem.

**Taints are node-side repulsion.** A taint says "keep pods off unless they opt in." `NoSchedule` blocks new pods, `PreferNoSchedule` is soft, and `NoExecute` also evicts already-running pods that don't tolerate it (with an optional `tolerationSeconds`). A toleration on a pod is only *permission* — it does not attract the pod anywhere. That's the classic confusion: tainting GPU nodes keeps normal work off them, but a GPU pod with only a toleration can still land on a cheap CPU node. To require placement you need node affinity, or a resource request only those nodes can satisfy. Kubernetes uses taints internally too: not-ready, unreachable, the pressure taints, and the unschedulable taint that `kubectl cordon` applies.

**Affinity is pod-side attraction.** `nodeSelector` is the hard, exact-match primitive; node affinity adds expressive operators and both `required...` and `preferred...` (weighted) forms. Pod affinity/anti-affinity places pods relative to *other pods* over a `topologyKey` — same zone as the cache, or never two replicas on the same host. Note that every one of these is `...IgnoredDuringExecution`: they're evaluated only at scheduling time, so relabelling a node never moves a running pod. Also, inter-pod affinity is computationally expensive and measurably slows scheduling on large clusters.

**Topology spread constraints** express *degree* of spreading, which anti-affinity cannot. Required anti-affinity is binary — at most one pod per domain — so 10 replicas across 3 zones leaves 7 pods Pending forever. `maxSkew: 1` over `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` says the busiest zone may hold at most one more pod than the emptiest, which is what people actually mean. `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` makes it hard; `ScheduleAnyway` demotes it to a scoring preference. The typical production pattern is hard spread across zones and soft spread across hostnames.

The tradeoff to mention: hard zone spread means that if one zone is full or down, new pods go Pending rather than piling into the healthy zones — you're explicitly choosing balance over availability, and sometimes `ScheduleAnyway` is the better answer.

Rounding it out: PriorityClass decides who wins when there isn't room (and by default may preempt lower-priority pods), and a PodDisruptionBudget is what stops drains and autoscaler scale-downs from removing your spread all at once.
followUps: If I taint my GPU nodes and add a toleration to my GPU pod, is the pod guaranteed to run on a GPU node?
Why is `requiredDuringScheduling` anti-affinity a bad way to spread 10 replicas across 3 zones?
What does `IgnoredDuringExecution` mean in practice?
How do node taints interact with DaemonSets?

interviewQA.q: Explain PV, PVC and StorageClass, and what `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` is for.
interviewQA.a:
A PersistentVolume is a cluster-scoped object representing a real piece of storage. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a namespaced *request* — size, access mode, class — and it's what a pod references. A StorageClass describes a kind of storage: which provisioner, what parameters, reclaim policy, expansion, binding mode. With dynamic provisioning, an unbound PVC referencing a class causes the external provisioner to create the real volume and a matching PV. Binding is exclusive and one-to-one.

`WaitForFirstConsumer` exists because of a real, common outage in multi-zone clusters. With the default `Immediate` binding, the volume is created the moment the PVC exists — say in zone A — and only later does the scheduler try to place the pod. If the pod can only run in zone B (because of affinity, taints, or simply where capacity exists), it can never attach that disk, and it sits Pending forever with a volume-node-affinity conflict. `WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until a pod using the claim has been scheduled, so the disk is created in the zone the pod actually landed in, respecting its constraints. Essentially every modern cloud StorageClass should use it. The corollary is that a PVC reporting "waiting for first consumer to be created before binding" is *normal*, not an error.

Other fields worth knowing: `reclaimPolicy` — `Delete` destroys the underlying volume when the PVC goes away (the default for most dynamic classes, and a good way to lose a database), `Retain` keeps it in `Released` state for manual recovery. `allowVolumeExpansion` lets you grow a PVC by editing its requested size; most CSI drivers support online expansion, and you can never shrink.

Access modes describe how many **nodes** can mount, not how many pods: `ReadWriteOnce` is one node (multiple pods on that node can share it), `ReadWriteMany` needs a filesystem backend like NFS/EFS/CephFS since most block storage can't do it, and `ReadWriteOncePod` restricts to exactly one pod. The classic bug here is a Deployment with an RWO PVC and a RollingUpdate strategy: the new pod lands on a different node and hits `Multi-Attach error for volume ... already exclusively attached to one node` until the old pod fully terminates. Use `Recreate`, a StatefulSet, or RWX storage.

Everything is implemented through CSI — a controller component doing create/delete/attach/snapshot and a node DaemonSet doing stage/mount — which is why storage failures surface as `FailedAttachVolume`/`FailedMount` events on the pod and are diagnosed in the CSI controller logs.
followUps: What does `Multi-Attach error` mean and how do you avoid it?
What happens to the data when you delete a PVC with reclaimPolicy Delete? How would you recover?
Why is a PVC stuck in Terminating, and what is the pvc-protection finalizer?
How do you expand a volume that's running out of space?

interviewQA.q: What happens when a worker node dies? What does Kubernetes do, and what doesn't it do?
interviewQA.a:
kubelet renews a Lease object roughly every 10 seconds as a heartbeat. When the node-lifecycle controller stops seeing renewals for the grace period (about 40 seconds by default), it sets the node's `Ready` condition to `Unknown` and applies the `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute` taint. Every pod carries a default 300-second toleration for that taint (injected by the DefaultTolerationSeconds admission plugin), so roughly five minutes after the node stopped responding, eviction begins.

Here's the part that catches people out: **the pods are marked for deletion but do not go away.** A pod deletion isn't finalised until a kubelet confirms the containers are gone, and there is no kubelet — so those pods sit in `Terminating` indefinitely. For a Deployment that's fine: the ReplicaSet sees fewer non-terminating pods than desired and creates replacements elsewhere, so you lose capacity for a few minutes and then recover. For a StatefulSet it's deliberately different: `mysql-0` is *not* recreated, because Kubernetes cannot distinguish "the node is dead" from "the node is partitioned but still running and still writing to its disk." Recreating the pod would risk two processes writing the same data. Similarly, RWO volumes can't be safely detached while the old node might still be using them.

To resolve it you have to **fence the node** — prove it's really dead and tell Kubernetes so. The supported mechanism is the `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taint, which lets the controllers force-detach volumes and complete pod deletion so replacements can be created. Force-deleting pods with `--grace-period=0 --force` achieves the same thing without any safety check, which is why it's a last resort for stateful workloads.

Things Kubernetes does **not** do: it doesn't reschedule running pods proactively (there's no rebalancing; a pod is bound to its node for life, and "rescheduling" always means delete-and-recreate); it doesn't repair the node; and it doesn't respect PodDisruptionBudgets here, because a crashed node is an *involuntary* disruption and PDBs only govern voluntary ones like drains.

The practical implications for design: run enough replicas spread across nodes and zones so losing one node is absorbed; keep `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and the eviction timeout in mind when reasoning about recovery time (roughly 40s detection plus 5 minutes toleration by default, which you can shorten per-pod with explicit tolerations); and for stateful systems rely on the application's own replication and failover, not on Kubernetes moving a disk.

How long does it take by default from node failure to pod eviction, and how would you shorten it?
Do PodDisruptionBudgets protect you here?

interviewQA.q: How would you safely drain a node for maintenance?
interviewQA.a:
`kubectl cordon <node>` first — that adds the `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable` taint so no new pods land there while you work, without touching anything running. Then `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data`.

The important mechanism is that drain doesn't delete pods; it calls the **Eviction API**, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets. If evicting a pod would push a workload below its budget, the eviction is rejected and drain retries, blocking until it becomes safe. That's the feature, not a bug — it's what stops a node upgrade from taking your last healthy replica. `--ignore-daemonsets` is required because DaemonSet pods are immediately recreated on the same node and tolerate the taints, so they'd block forever; `--delete-emptydir-data` acknowledges you're destroying local scratch data; and you should set a `--timeout` so a stuck drain fails visibly instead of hanging in CI.

Prerequisites for this to actually be safe: PDBs on every important workload (with `maxUnavailable: 1` or a percentage — never `minAvailable` equal to the replica count, which blocks all drains permanently); enough spare capacity or a cluster autoscaler so evicted pods have somewhere to go, otherwise they just go Pending; multiple replicas spread across nodes; and graceful shutdown with a `preStop` sleep, because eviction is a pod deletion and hits exactly the same endpoint-removal race as a rolling update.

Then do the maintenance and `kubectl uncordon <node>`. Note that uncordoning doesn't rebalance anything — the pods that moved stay where they went. If distribution matters, you either rely on topology spread for future scheduling or run something like the descheduler.

Watch out for the things that make a drain hang: a PDB showing `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0` (either because it's too strict or because the workload is already unhealthy, so evicting even one pod would breach the floor); bare pods with no controller, which drain refuses to evict without `--force` since nothing would recreate them; long `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` on stateful pods; and PVC attach delays as volumes detach from this node and attach elsewhere. `kubectl get pdb -A` and `kubectl describe pdb` are the first things to check when it stalls.
followUps: Why does drain need `--ignore-daemonsets`?
What's the difference between the Eviction API and `kubectl delete pod`?
A drain has been stuck for an hour. What do you check?
Do PDBs protect against a node crashing?

interviewQA.q: Is a namespace a security boundary? How do you isolate tenants in a shared cluster?
interviewQA.a:
No. A namespace is a scope for names and a place to *attach* policy, but by default a pod in namespace A can open a TCP connection to a pod IP in namespace B, and a compromised workload can reach anything the flat pod network allows. Isolation is something you compose on top.

The layers, roughly in order of how often they're forgotten:

**RBAC** — Roles and RoleBindings scoped per namespace, with a distinct ServiceAccount per workload and `automountServiceAccountToken: false` where the pod doesn't call the API. Remember that `get secrets` and `create pods` in a namespace are both close to owning that namespace.

**NetworkPolicy** — a default-deny baseline per namespace, then explicit allows. Non-optional if you care about lateral movement. Don't forget DNS egress, or the namespace goes dark.

**ResourceQuota and LimitRange** — so one tenant can't consume the cluster's CPU/memory, PVC storage, or LoadBalancer count, and so pods can't request absurd amounts. Note the coupling: a quota on `requests.cpu` makes every pod that omits requests get rejected, so you need a LimitRange supplying defaults.

**Pod Security admission** at `restricted` per namespace, which blocks privileged containers, host namespaces, hostPath mounts, and privilege escalation — the things that turn a container compromise into a node compromise.

**Node-level separation** — taints plus affinity to keep tenants on separate node pools, so a kernel-level escape doesn't cross tenants; plus resource isolation from Guaranteed QoS.

**The control plane surface** — admission policy on what images may run, blocking the cloud metadata endpoint via NetworkPolicy egress rules, and audit logging.

And then the honest caveat, which is what a good interviewer is really after: for *hostile* multi-tenancy — running code you don't trust — none of this is sufficient, because all pods share one kernel. A container escape via a kernel bug crosses every namespace boundary you've built. For that you need separate clusters, or at minimum sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata Containers) on dedicated node pools. Soft multi-tenancy between cooperating internal teams is what the namespace toolkit is designed for; hard multi-tenancy against adversaries is a different problem.
followUps: What specifically does Pod Security's `restricted` profile prevent?
Why is `create pods` in a namespace nearly equivalent to owning it?
How would you stop workloads from reaching the cloud metadata endpoint?
When would you insist on separate clusters instead?

interviewQA.q: What is etcd's role, how does it fail, and how do you back it up?
interviewQA.a:
etcd is the only durable state in a Kubernetes cluster: every object lives there, under `/registry/...`, and only the API server talks to it. Rebuild every node and every binary and you still have your cluster if you have etcd; lose etcd with no snapshot and the cluster's contents are gone.

It's a Raft-consensus store, so writes need a majority to commit. Three members tolerate one failure, five tolerate two, and even numbers buy nothing — four members still need three up. Lose quorum and writes stop: no scheduling, no rollouts, no endpoint updates. Notably, *running pods keep running* — kubelet doesn't need the control plane to keep containers alive — so an etcd outage is usually a "the cluster is frozen" event rather than an immediate user-visible outage, which is a nice nuance to mention.

Failure modes worth naming. **Disk latency**: every commit is an fsync to the WAL on each voting member, so fsync latency becomes API write latency directly. Put etcd on network storage or a noisy shared disk and you get repeated leader elections and `request timed out` errors. Watch `etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds`, `etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds`, and `etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total`. **Space**: etcd is MVCC, old revisions are kept until compaction, and compaction only frees space inside the file — you need defragmentation to return it to the filesystem. Cross the default 2 GiB backend quota and etcd raises a `NOSPACE` alarm and refuses writes, which presents as a totally broken cluster. Runaway growth usually means a controller hot-looping writes or something storing huge objects. **Latency between members**: stretching etcd across regions is a reliable way to make everything slow.

Backups are `etcdctl snapshot save` against a live member, with the CA/cert/key — one file, the whole cluster. Take them on a schedule, store them off-cluster, and *test restores*, because a restore is a genuinely disruptive procedure: you stop the API servers, `etcdctl snapshot restore` into a new data directory to form a fresh single-member cluster, restart, then re-add members one at a time. Also note a restore rolls the entire cluster back in time, so anything created after the snapshot vanishes while the real-world resources it created (cloud load balancers, disks) do not.

Two security points: enable encryption at rest with a KMS provider, since Secrets are otherwise plaintext in the datastore, and protect etcd's client and peer TLS as carefully as cluster-admin, because an etcd client certificate is effectively read/write access to everything with no RBAC in the way.
followUps: Why 3 or 5 members and not 4?
What happens to running pods when etcd loses quorum?
What's the difference between compaction and defragmentation?
What are the risks of restoring from a snapshot taken an hour ago?

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between a Job, a CronJob and a Deployment, and is a CronJob exactly-once?
interviewQA.a:
A Deployment is a steady-state controller: it keeps N pods running forever and its pods must have `restartPolicy: Always`. A Job is run-to-completion: it runs pods until a required number succeed and then stops, with `restartPolicy` restricted to `OnFailure` or `Never`. A CronJob is a thin controller that creates Jobs on a schedule.

The Job knobs that matter: `completions` (how many successes are needed) and `parallelism` (how many at once) — `completions: 100, parallelism: 10` is a batch of 100 processed ten at a time, while omitting completions and setting parallelism gives a worker-pool that finishes when any worker exits successfully. `completionMode: Indexed` gives each pod a fixed index so you can statically shard work. `backoffLimit` (default 6) is how many pod failures are tolerated, with exponential backoff up to six minutes between retries, and `activeDeadlineSeconds` is a hard wall-clock cap that overrides it. Newer `podFailurePolicy` rules let you fail fast on a permanent error code and *not* count infrastructure preemptions against the backoff limit, which matters a lot on spot capacity. And `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` is how you stop thousands of Completed pods accumulating and bloating etcd.

Note the `restartPolicy` interaction: `OnFailure` restarts the container in place in the same pod (fast, but a crash-looping container burns wall clock before it counts as a pod failure), while `Never` creates a new pod per attempt and leaves the failed ones around for inspection.

CronJob fields: `schedule` plus `timeZone`; `concurrencyPolicy` of `Allow` (default), `Forbid` (skip if the previous run is still going), or `Replace`; `startingDeadlineSeconds` bounding how late a missed run may start; history limits; and `suspend` to pause scheduling during an incident without deleting anything.

And no — **a CronJob is not exactly-once.** It can miss a window if the control plane is down or the starting deadline passes (and if more than 100 schedules are missed it gives up rather than stampeding), and it can in principle create two Jobs for one schedule. The guarantee is roughly at-least-once, best-effort on time. So your job must be idempotent: a unique run key, a lock, or an upsert. Never assume a nightly billing run happened exactly once.

One more classic: before native sidecar containers, an injected mesh proxy would keep running after the main container exited, so the pod never completed and the Job hung forever. Native sidecars (init containers with `restartPolicy: Always`) fix this properly.
followUps: What does `backoffLimit` count, and how does it interact with `restartPolicy: OnFailure`?
How do you stop completed Job pods from accumulating?
Your hourly job now takes 70 minutes. What does each concurrencyPolicy do?
How do you make a nightly job safe against being run twice?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a DaemonSet and a Deployment, and when do you actually need one?
interviewQA.a:
A Deployment runs N interchangeable pods anywhere the scheduler likes; a DaemonSet runs exactly one pod on every node matching its selector, *including nodes that don't exist yet* — add a node and the pod appears immediately. That "future nodes" property is the whole reason infrastructure ships this way: CNI agents, kube-proxy, log collectors, node metrics exporters, CSI node plugins, security agents.

Mechanically, DaemonSet pods are scheduled by the normal scheduler — the controller creates each pod with node affinity pinning it to one specific node. So they respect resource fit, priority and preemption like anything else, which is why infrastructure DaemonSets should set `priorityClassName: system-node-critical`; otherwise a full node leaves your log shipper Pending. The controller also automatically adds tolerations for `not-ready`, `unreachable`, the pressure taints, and `unschedulable`, so agents stay alive on nodes that are in trouble and are not removed by `kubectl drain` (hence `--ignore-daemonsets`). It does *not* add tolerations for control-plane taints or your custom taints — you add those yourself.

Use a DaemonSet only when the workload is genuinely per-node: reading `/var/log/containers` via hostPath, listening on the node's network, programming the node's kernel, or exposing node hardware. If you use one just to "have a copy everywhere" for a stateless HTTP service, you've tied your replica count to your node count and given up autoscaling — that should be a Deployment with an HPA.

Two operational points. Resource requests are multiplied by the node count, so an extra 200 MiB per pod across 500 nodes is 100 GiB of capacity you can no longer schedule apps into; size them carefully. And updates walk node by node with `maxUnavailable` defaulting to 1, which on a large cluster with a slow-starting agent can take hours — `maxUnavailable: 10%` is a normal tuning.

Security is the last thing worth raising: DaemonSets typically need hostPath mounts, host networking, or elevated capabilities, which makes them the highest-value target in the cluster. A compromised agent with `hostPath: /` is a node takeover, and since it runs on every node, it's a cluster takeover. Keep the image minimal, the RBAC tight, and the Pod Security exemption narrow rather than cluster-wide.
followUps: Which tolerations does the DaemonSet controller add automatically, and why?
Why does `kubectl drain` need `--ignore-daemonsets`?
How would you run a DaemonSet only on GPU nodes?
Why can't you use an HPA with a DaemonSet?

interviewQA.q: How does kube-proxy make a ClusterIP work, and what are the differences between its modes?
interviewQA.a:
A ClusterIP is a virtual address that nothing listens on. There's no process bound to it and no interface holding it — it exists only as rules in each node's packet-processing path. When a pod connects to the ClusterIP, the node's kernel DNATs the destination to a real pod IP before the packet leaves, and un-NATs the reply. That's why you generally can't ping a ClusterIP and never see it on the wire between nodes.

kube-proxy is the DaemonSet that writes those rules. It watches Services and EndpointSlices through the API server and reprograms the node's dataplane on every change.

In **iptables** mode (the long-standing default), it writes a chain per Service under `KUBE-SERVICES` that jumps to one chain per endpoint, using the `statistic random probability` module to select uniformly. It's simple and battle-tested, but the rules form a linear structure and a change means recomputing and reloading a large ruleset, so on clusters with tens of thousands of services/endpoints, update latency and CPU become a real problem. In **IPVS** mode, it programs the kernel's in-kernel L4 load balancer, which uses hash-based lookup rather than sequential matching, scales far better with service count, and supports real algorithms (round-robin, least-connection, source hashing). A newer **nftables** mode (beta from v1.31) gives iptables-like semantics with much better update and lookup performance and is where the project is heading. Separately, eBPF-based CNIs like Cilium can replace kube-proxy entirely, implementing service load balancing in BPF programs at the socket layer, which also removes a lot of conntrack pressure.

Whichever mode, the backends come from **EndpointSlices** — the modern replacement for the single Endpoints object, which had to be rewritten in full on every change and produced megabyte-scale writes on large services when one pod flapped. Slices cap at 100 endpoints each by default and carry per-endpoint `ready`/`serving`/`terminating` conditions plus topology hints.

Two behavioural facts to close with. Load balancing is **per connection**, not per request — so a single long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connection pins to one backend. And `externalTrafficPolicy` controls the external path: `Cluster` (default) lets any node forward to a pod anywhere, giving even distribution but SNATing away the client IP and adding a hop; `Local` only accepts traffic on nodes running a backend pod, preserving the client IP and removing the hop, but making load proportional to pods-per-node and relying on the LB's `healthCheckNodePort` to stop sending to empty nodes.
